questions.scenario: A media archive stores 80 million video-frame embeddings. Curators run similarity search a few times per week. The team refuses to manage clusters and wants to pay only when they query.
questions.question: Which vector store BEST fits this pattern?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless with k-NN for always-on low latency
Amazon S3 vector buckets and vector indexes
Amazon DynamoDB items scanned by Lambda cosine similarity
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL pgvector on a Multi-AZ instance

questions.explanation: Infrequent search + no infrastructure + pay-per-use is the S3 Vectors pattern from the official sample.

incorrectExplanations.a: Serverless OpenSearch still bills search capacity; it wins when queries are frequent.
incorrectExplanations.c: Lambda cosine over DynamoDB items is not an index. Native DynamoDB vector indexes exist for operational data already in DynamoDB — not an 80M rare-query archive.
incorrectExplanations.d: RDS is provisioned infrastructure.

questions.scenario: A RAG chatbot must run hybrid keyword + vector search at high QPS during business hours. Operational simplicity of S3 is attractive, but users complain that exact SKU matches are missed.
questions.question: Which store is the BETTER fit?

options.text: Amazon S3 Vectors alone
Amazon OpenSearch (Serverless or managed) with hybrid search
Amazon DocumentDB text indexes
Amazon Macie

questions.explanation: Frequent, low-latency, hybrid/keyword needs OpenSearch. S3 Vectors is the infrequent/cost path, not SKU-heavy high QPS.

incorrectExplanations.a: S3 Vectors is for infrequent k-NN, not hybrid high QPS.
incorrectExplanations.c: DocumentDB is not the exam’s enterprise/hybrid search answer.
incorrectExplanations.d: Macie classifies sensitive data; it does not retrieve SKUs.

questions.scenario: A Knowledge Base ingest job finishes with some PDFs missing from retrieval. The team needs per-file failure reasons such as EMBEDDING_FAILED.
questions.question: Where should they look FIRST?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail management events for bedrock:*
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs
Knowledge base APPLICATION_LOGS in CloudWatch Logs Insights
CloudWatch Application Signals service map

questions.explanation: KB vended APPLICATION_LOGS track each file in an ingestion job. CloudTrail is API audit; invocation logs are chat; Application Signals is APM.

incorrectExplanations.a: CloudTrail will not say why a PDF failed to embed.
incorrectExplanations.b: Invocation logging is inference, not ingest.
incorrectExplanations.d: Application Signals does not instrument KB crawlers.

questions.scenario: An app must halt Claude output as soon as the model prints the token </json>.
questions.question: Which control is reliable?

options.text: Set temperature to 0
Raise top-k so </json> is more likely
Add stopSequences: ["</json>"] on the inference call
Instruct the model in the user prompt to stop at </json>

questions.explanation: Stop sequences terminate generation when the phrase is emitted. Sampling knobs and prompt instructions do not.

incorrectExplanations.a: Temperature changes randomness, not the stop point.
incorrectExplanations.b: top-k is sampling diversity.
incorrectExplanations.d: Instruction-following is not a hard stop.

questions.scenario: The blotter calls one Amazon Bedrock foundation model with Converse. During business hours it receives ThrottlingException / Too many requests. Overnight the desk is idle. Compliance requires the same model ID — they will not route easy prompts to a sibling. The team wants a native Bedrock lever, the same API shape, and must not pay for reserved Model Units at 3 a.m. A homemade Lambda that retries us-west-2 would work but they want AWS to spread the load.
questions.question: Which inference mode is MOST cost-effective for this spiky, same-FM workload?

options.text: Cross-Region inference with a geographic inference profile (us.… / eu.…) on the same foundation model
Provisioned Throughput sized to the weekday peak and left running all month
Intelligent prompt routing across two models in the same family
A Lambda that catches 429s and retries a second Region with a hand-built client

questions.explanation: Capacity and which model answers are different knobs. Spiky on-demand traffic that must keep the same FM is cross-Region inference: an inference profile, Bedrock may serve the same model from another Region in that geography, still token-priced. Prompt routing changes the writer. Provisioned Throughput is hourly Model Units for flat dedicated load. A DIY Regional retry is the same idea with you owning the failover.

incorrectExplanations.b: PT is the right shape for predictable high utilization. Paying peak MUs through the night is the wrong bill for a spike. You did not graduate off Bedrock by buying PT; you bought the wrong SKU.
incorrectExplanations.c: Intelligent prompt routing picks a small or large model in a family at runtime (cost/quality). The stem forbade swapping models. Routing is not extra quota for one FM.
incorrectExplanations.d: Works, but you own retries, health, and Region lists. CRI is native Bedrock doing the spreading on the same API.

questions.scenario: Security requires every Converse and InvokeModel call to attach a named Bedrock guardrail. They want no extra proxy.
questions.question: Which control enforces this most efficiently?

options.text: IAM condition bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier on those actions
IAM conditions GuardrailIdentifier and PromptRouterArn together
Lambda that injects a guardrail ID from Parameter Store
A system prompt that says to follow the guardrail

questions.explanation: IAM bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier denies calls that omit the guardrail. PromptRouterArn is unrelated. Lambda is extra ops. Prompts are not enforcement.

incorrectExplanations.b: PromptRouterArn does not enforce guardrails.
incorrectExplanations.c: Stores an ID; does not deny unguarded calls by itself.
incorrectExplanations.d: Not a control.

questions.scenario: A guardrail blocks some tickets. The developer must see whether Content, Topic, or SensitiveInformation policy fired.
questions.question: Which configuration provides that dimension?

options.text: Invocation logging + GuardrailContentSource alarms
guardrailConfig trace enabled + InvocationsIntervened filtered by GuardrailPolicyType
A Bedrock model evaluation job with toxicity metrics
X-Ray service map

questions.explanation: PolicyType is ContentPolicy vs TopicPolicy vs SensitiveInformationPolicy. ContentSource is only input vs output. Eval jobs are offline.

incorrectExplanations.a: ContentSource is where, not which policy.
incorrectExplanations.c: Evaluation is not live intervention tracing.
incorrectExplanations.d: X-Ray will not name the guardrail policy.

questions.scenario: After a Lambda dependency bump, a RAG app answers “no relevant information found.” CloudWatch shows no errors. X-Ray shows successful InvokeModel. OpenSearch is green with normal latency.
questions.question: What MOST likely happened?

options.text: The Lambda role lost bedrock:InvokeModel
Temperature was increased
Query embeddings now use a different model or version than the index
All vectors were deleted from the index

questions.explanation: Silent empty retrieval with a healthy cluster and successful FM calls is embedding-space mismatch. IAM would error. Deleted indexes would not look healthy with normal latency.

incorrectExplanations.a: Would throw AccessDenied.
incorrectExplanations.b: Affects generation style, not retrieval emptiness.
incorrectExplanations.d: Would surface as failed or empty-index behavior, not a healthy cluster story.

questions.scenario: S3 is the KB data source. New and deleted objects must update the vector store within seconds, including during bursty uploads.
questions.question: Which architecture is event-driven AND resilient?

options.text: EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes calling StartIngestionJob
S3 event notifications to SQS, Lambda calling IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments and DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments
S3 event notifications invoking Lambda directly with those same APIs
A Step Functions sync every hour

questions.explanation: Per-object APIs plus SQS buffering match the official sample. Direct Lambda lacks retry buffer. Scheduler + StartIngestionJob is delayed batch sync.

incorrectExplanations.a: Not event-driven; delayed; scans.
incorrectExplanations.c: No queue — bursts can drop events.
incorrectExplanations.d: Hourly is not “as soon as possible.”

questions.scenario: Support emails in S3 contain SSNs. A mobile search app must never return those SSNs.
questions.question: Which pipeline is appropriate?

options.text: Index in Kendra first; add a Bedrock system prompt that says to hide PII
Amazon Macie findings as the search index
Amazon Comprehend PII redaction, then Amazon Kendra on the redacted objects
Amazon Textract plus DocumentDB queries

questions.explanation: Redact with Comprehend, then search the clean corpus with Kendra. Prompts are not controls. Macie discovers; Textract/DocumentDB are the wrong pair for email NL search.

incorrectExplanations.a: PII is already in the index; prompts can be bypassed.
incorrectExplanations.b: Macie is discovery, not a search engine.
incorrectExplanations.d: Textract is for scans; DocumentDB is not NL enterprise search.

questions.scenario: Users submit a 40 MB text file of image prompts and need GPU image generation within 15 minutes, on demand.
questions.question: Which SageMaker option meets payload, GPU, time, and on-demand together?

options.text: Batch Transform started from Lambda
Real-Time Inference on an accelerated instance
Asynchronous Inference on an accelerated instance
Serverless Inference on a general-purpose instance

questions.explanation: Async supports up to 1 GB and long runtimes with GPUs. Real-Time caps at 25 MB. Serverless has no GPU. Batch is offline.

incorrectExplanations.a: Not an on-demand per-user wait.
incorrectExplanations.b: 25 MB payload limit.
incorrectExplanations.d: No GPU; 4 MB / 60 s.

questions.scenario: A DJL-served LLM on an 8-GPU instance fits in 4 GPUs. Production sequences are much shorter than max_seq. Concurrency per instance is low.
questions.question: Which TWO changes improve utilization? (Select TWO)

options.text: Turn on speculative decoding as the primary utilization fix
Set tensor parallel degree to 8 so one replica uses every GPU
Set tensor parallel degree to 4 so two replicas share the instance
Reduce maximum sequence length to raise rolling batch size

questions.explanation: Degree 4 packs two copies. Smaller max sequence frees memory for batch. Degree 8 under-packs. Speculative decoding is latency, not packing.

incorrectExplanations.a: Wrong knob for GPU packing.
incorrectExplanations.b: One replica on all 8 GPUs wastes the fact that 4 are enough.

questions.scenario: Python agent code must run on AgentCore Runtime with automatic /invocations and /ping, JSON and long streaming, minimal Docker work.
questions.question: Which TWO approaches minimize operations? (Select TWO)

options.text: AgentCore SDK @app.entrypoint
AgentCore starter toolkit packaging and CreateAgentRuntime
Hand-written FastAPI with those routes plus your own images
SageMaker real-time custom inference container

questions.explanation: Official sample pair: SDK server + starter toolkit deploy. FastAPI and SageMaker add container/ops tax.

incorrectExplanations.c: You own the server and images.
incorrectExplanations.d: Wrong runtime and more ops.

questions.scenario: A new Bedrock model may replace production only if it is measurably better. Each step needs approval before the next.
questions.question: Order the evaluation workflow.

options.text: Implement automated quality gates with AWS Step Functions
Analyze results and write the evaluation report
Define metrics for relevance, factual accuracy, and fluency
Create a test dataset with diverse scenarios and edge cases
Run A/B tests of the new model against production

questions.explanation: Metrics, then dataset, then A/B, then automated gates, then the report. Gates cannot run before you know what to measure.

questions.scenario: A Bedrock RAG app retrieves many related chunks but the best paragraph is ranked fifth. The team wants managed features, not a custom ranker.
questions.question: Which TWO steps improve ranking with the least ops? (Select TWO)

options.text: Amazon Bedrock reranker models with OpenSearch
OpenSearch Learning to Rank with an XGBoost judgment list
Knowledge Bases hybrid search (vector + keyword)
Aurora pgvector plus a hand-written scoring formula

questions.explanation: Official pair: managed reranker + hybrid search. LTR and homemade Aurora scoring are high ops.

incorrectExplanations.b: LTR plugin is the distractor from the sample.
incorrectExplanations.d: You own the ranker.

questions.scenario: Regulators require prompt approval workflows and seven years of immutable prompt/completion records, with little custom code.
questions.question: Which TWO pieces meet both needs? (Select TWO)

options.text: Bedrock Prompt Management with multi-stage approvals
CloudTrail Lake with 7-year retention of API metadata
Bedrock invocation logging to S3 with Object Lock compliance mode
Prompt templates in DynamoDB with item-level IAM

questions.explanation: Prompt Management governs templates. Invocation logging plus Object Lock keeps the bodies. CloudTrail is not content. DynamoDB is a homemade workflow.

incorrectExplanations.b: CloudTrail does not store prompts and completions.
incorrectExplanations.d: High operational overhead.

questions.scenario: An NVDA earnings-blotter Lambda in us-east-1 calls a single Bedrock FM. On print morning it hits Too many requests for about three hours. Legal forbids changing models. The team wants native Bedrock, the same Converse call, and must not rent idle capacity overnight. Custom models are not in scope — this is a base FM.
questions.question: Which lever increases peak throughput MOST cost-effectively without changing the writer?

options.text: Intelligent prompt routing to a cheaper model in the family during the spike
Provisioned Throughput sized to print-morning peak
Move the workload to a SageMaker real-time endpoint so it can autoscale
A geographic cross-Region inference profile for the same foundation model

questions.explanation: Print-morning burst + same FM + token pricing is CRI. Inference profiles (us.…, eu.…, global) keep the model ID’s writer and let Bedrock use spare capacity in the geography. Custom models cannot use CRI; this stem is a base FM. PT and SageMaker are heavier bills or a different host.

incorrectExplanations.a: Routing changes which model answers. Compliance said same FM. Also routing is not a quota boost for one ID.
incorrectExplanations.b: Hourly Model Units through the night for a three-hour spike. Right lever for 24/7 dedicated load, wrong bill here.
incorrectExplanations.c: Staying on Bedrock is the default. CRI is Bedrock’s peak relief. SageMaker is for a training loop or a runtime Bedrock will not host.

questions.scenario: The blotter’s JSON is sloppy even with few-shot prompts. A Knowledge Base already holds the 10-Ks. The team fine-tunes a Bedrock FM on labeled examples so it writes house JSON. Traffic is variable (quiet night, print-morning spike). The custom model and Region support Custom Model Deployment. They do not want to pay hourly Model Units overnight.
questions.question: How should they invoke the custom model?

options.text: On-demand InvokeModel using the fine-tune job ID as if it were a base foundation model
A cross-Region inference profile pointed at the custom model
Intelligent prompt routing between the custom model and the base FM to save quota
A Custom Model Deployment: invoke the deployment ARN as modelId and pay on-demand tokens

questions.explanation: Custom models are no longer PT-or-nothing. Where the model and Region support it, Custom Model Deployment lets you invoke a deployment ARN as modelId on on-demand tokens — the right shape for variable traffic. PT remains dedicated, predictable capacity, and the path when CMD is not supported. Custom / fine-tuned models still cannot use CRI. A raw job ID is not an on-demand base-FM ID.

incorrectExplanations.a: You do not call a custom artifact like a catalog FM ID on shared on-demand. Use a Custom Model Deployment ARN or Provisioned Throughput.
incorrectExplanations.b: CRI is for on-demand foundation models. Custom models cannot ride inference profiles.
incorrectExplanations.c: Prompt routing is a same-family cost/quality pick at runtime, not how you host a fine-tune.

questions.scenario: Product wants to flip the blotter from Claude Haiku to Claude Sonnet on Friday without shipping a new Lambda zip. Both models are already enabled in the account. The application contract is generate(messages, options). They will re-run the same 100-question eval after the flip. The model ID today is hardcoded in the container image.
questions.question: Which approach changes the model ID with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Fine-tune Haiku until it behaves like Sonnet so the ID never changes
Store the model ID in AWS AppConfig (or Parameter Store) and read it at invoke time
Put Provisioned Throughput on both models and bake a new alias into the next container deploy
Rebuild the function with a hardcoded Sonnet ID and deploy the zip

questions.explanation: Skill 1.2.2 is dynamic model selection and provider switching without a code change. AppConfig (or Parameter Store) holds the modelId; Friday is a config flip. Converse keeps the message shape across providers but does not make every model identical — that is why they still re-eval. Do not bury MODEL in 17 Lambdas.

incorrectExplanations.a: Fine-tuning changes weights and behavior. It is not how you point the app at a different catalog FM.
incorrectExplanations.c: PT is a capacity SKU. If the ID still lives in the image, you still deploy. Aliases belong in config, not in a container rebuild.
incorrectExplanations.d: That is a code deploy, which the stem forbade.

questions.scenario: An investor-relations team wants a two-week proof of concept: a chatbot that summarizes NVDA earnings transcripts and cites the paragraph it used. Finance will not fund GPU clusters. Legal forbids custom model weights for this demo. The team has already pasted a real transcript paragraph into the Bedrock playground and the answer looked useful. They need the least operational overhead that can still fail the idea on citations, not merely return a 200 from Converse.
questions.question: Which starting design meets the PoC with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker training jobs that fine-tune a model, then a real-time GPU endpoint
Amazon EKS with a DJL Serving cluster so the demo can scale later
Amazon Bedrock on-demand (Converse) plus a Knowledge Base over the transcripts in S3
Fine-tune Amazon Titan on every historical 10-K, then invoke the custom model on-demand

questions.explanation: Skill 1.1.2: a PoC exists to learn on a clock. Exam phrasing like least operational overhead, rapid prototype, or proof of concept maps to Bedrock on-demand. Citations over your docs add a Knowledge Base — still Bedrock, still token-priced, still no cluster. A playground paste is step one; the KB is the next least-ops step when the stem requires grounding. You do not start on SageMaker, EKS, or a fine-tune to prove the idea.

incorrectExplanations.a: SageMaker is the box you size: training loop, instance type, endpoint, container. Use it when Bedrock cannot host the model or you need a long or large GPU job. It is the wrong kitchen for a two-week citation demo.
incorrectExplanations.b: EKS (or EC2) plus GPU nodes is maximum control and maximum operations. The curriculum fork is Bedrock first, SageMaker if you must train or host your image, EKS only if both refuse the runtime. Scaling later is not a PoC requirement.
incorrectExplanations.d: Fine-tuning changes how the model writes (JSON, tone). It does not put this quarter's transcript in the weights, and weights have no footnote. The stem asked for citations and forbade custom weights. That knowledge belongs in a Knowledge Base.

questions.scenario: IR drops a 90-minute NVDA earnings-call MP3 into S3. The blotter must retrieve similar *passages* later with a text embedding model and a Knowledge Base over transcripts. Legal wants an exact searchable transcript, not semantic search over the audio waveform. The team has already enabled a text FM.
questions.question: What is the FIRST processing step that matches the downstream model?

options.text: Invoke Titan Text Embeddings on the MP3 bytes so the Knowledge Base can index the audio file directly
Run Amazon Transcribe to text, then chunk and embed the transcript
Attach a Bedrock Guardrail to the S3 bucket so the webcast cannot contain PII before anyone listens
Load the MP3 as a binary document into OpenSearch and search it with BM25

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.2: pick the path from the job, not the file extension. Exact searchable transcript plus a text embedder means Transcribe first, then chunk and embed. Native multimodal embeddings are a different path when you search the audio itself. Same MP3, different downstream model.

incorrectExplanations.a: Text embedders do not take a webcast blob. That call fails before retrieval starts. Multimodal embeddings would be right only if the job were semantic search over the audio, which this stem forbade.
incorrectExplanations.c: Guardrails filter model I/O. They do not transcribe, and they do not attach to a bucket as a processing step.
incorrectExplanations.d: OpenSearch is a later shelf (1.4). A binary MP3 is not a keyword document. You still need speech-to-text for passage search.

questions.scenario: The team swapped the blotter to a new embedding model. Retrieve quality collapsed. Chunking is unchanged.
questions.question: What fixes the drift?

options.text: Prefix every query with the new model name
Re-embed the corpus with the new model and replace the index
Raise temperature on RetrieveAndGenerate
Switch the vector store from OpenSearch to DynamoDB

questions.explanation: Query space must match index space. Reindex. Prompt prefixes do not rotate an embedding space.

incorrectExplanations.a: Q6 trap.
incorrectExplanations.c: Decoding knobs are not retrieval.
incorrectExplanations.d: Swapping stores does not rotate embedding space. Re-embed.

questions.scenario: Every blotter call resends the same 4k-token IR system prompt plus a short user question. Token cost is dominated by that prefix.
questions.question: Which cost lever fits FIRST?

options.text: Bedrock prompt caching on the stable prefix
Provisioned Throughput sized to overnight idle
Raise temperature to shorten answers
Move the FM to Lambda in-process

questions.explanation: Prompt caching is the coat check for a repeated prefix. PT does not shrink tokens. Temperature is not a cost control.

incorrectExplanations.b: Wrong bill shape.
incorrectExplanations.c: Does not cache the prefix; may worsen quality.
incorrectExplanations.d: Lambda does not host the FM.

questions.scenario: The workflow is always: retrieve two 10-K exhibits, summarize, email IR. No extra tools. Ops wants a visual graph, not a ReAct loop.
questions.question: Which product implements a fixed retrieve-summarize-email graph with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: AgentCore Runtime with a custom FastAPI server
Amazon Q Developer in the IDE
Bedrock Agents with six action groups
Bedrock Prompt Flows

questions.explanation: Fixed prompt DAG = Prompt Flows. Agents are for tool-choosing loops. FastAPI is extra ops. Q Developer is code.

incorrectExplanations.a: Q10 trap pattern — you do not hand-wire HTTP when you do not even need AgentCore.
incorrectExplanations.b: Wrong Q.
incorrectExplanations.c: ReAct is overkill for a fixed three-step graph.

questions.scenario: A team packaged an open-weight LLM in a DJL Serving container that requires GPU memory. Interactive chat must return in a few seconds. A teammate proposed Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate.
questions.question: Which hosting option meets GPU and managed-container needs?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock on-demand Converse for an arbitrary DJL image
Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on a GPU instance with the custom container
AWS Lambda with 10 GB memory loading the weights
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate with the DJL container

questions.explanation: Fargate has no GPU. Lambda has no GPU for FM hosting. SageMaker real-time runs your DJL container on a GPU instance.

incorrectExplanations.a: Bedrock does not run an arbitrary DJL Serving image you already packaged.
incorrectExplanations.c: Lambda cannot host a GPU LLM.
incorrectExplanations.d: Fargate does not provide GPU instance types.

questions.scenario: A new FM must replace prod only if it is measurably better. Each step needs approval before the next.
questions.question: What is the FIRST step?

options.text: Stand up Step Functions quality gates
Write the evaluation report
Define metrics such as relevance, factual accuracy, and fluency
A/B the new model against production

questions.explanation: Q17: metrics first. Gates, A/B, and the report consume the scoreboard.

incorrectExplanations.a: Gates with nothing to measure.
incorrectExplanations.b: Report with no tests.
incorrectExplanations.d: A/B against what scores?

questions.scenario: Security wants to know whether a denied-topic rule fired on the user prompt or on the model completion.
questions.question: Which artifact answers that?

options.text: CloudTrail InvokeModel events
A Bedrock Model Evaluation job
The guardrail trace ContentSource (INPUT vs OUTPUT) plus PolicyType
OpenSearch slow logs

questions.explanation: Q19: PolicyType is the rule family; ContentSource is input vs output. Eval jobs and CloudTrail do not replace the trace.

incorrectExplanations.a: No policy-level INPUT/OUTPUT split.
incorrectExplanations.b: Offline quality lab, not a live guardrail debug.
incorrectExplanations.d: Wrong product.

questions.scenario: Analyst cell numbers appear in some transcript files. They must not be searchable in Amazon Kendra.
questions.question: Which order is required?

options.text: Index in Kendra first, then attach a Guardrail
Detect and redact PII, then index the cleaned text in Kendra
Enable Macie on the Kendra index
Raise the FM temperature so it ignores phone numbers

questions.explanation: Q14: redact then index. Guardrails on the FM do not unsay an index that already stored the numbers.

incorrectExplanations.a: You indexed the PII.
incorrectExplanations.c: Macie crawls S3, not a Kendra index, and still would not define ingest order.
incorrectExplanations.d: Not a privacy control.

questions.scenario: Developers want inline completions and PR review in the IDE. IR wants a separate chat over SharePoint with user ACLs.
questions.question: Which pairing matches IDE coding assistance versus employee chat over company documents with ACLs?

options.text: QuickSight for both
Q Business for the IDE; Q Developer for SharePoint
Bedrock Agents for both
Q Developer for the IDE; Q Business for enterprise chat with ACLs

questions.explanation: Two different Qs: Developer = code; Business = badge-aware enterprise knowledge.

incorrectExplanations.a: BI, not IDE or wiki chat.
incorrectExplanations.b: Swapped.
incorrectExplanations.c: You can build it; the stem asked for the prebuilt products.

questions.scenario: RetrieveAndGenerate started returning empty context. Invocation logging is already on. Sync might have failed.
questions.question: What else must you enable to debug ingest and retrieve?

options.text: Knowledge Base logging
CloudTrail Lake only
A Bedrock Model Evaluation job
Macie

questions.explanation: Q2: Knowledge Base logging is a different switch from invocation logging. It is the librarian’s notebook.

incorrectExplanations.b: Who called the API, not why retrieve was empty.
incorrectExplanations.c: Quality lab, not ingest debug.
incorrectExplanations.d: S3 sensitive-data discovery.

questions.scenario: Legal's design constraint is that NVDA 10-Ks and Bedrock inference traffic must stay on the AWS network in this VPC. The blotter already calls Converse from a Lambda in a private subnet. The team must not send Bedrock requests out a NAT Gateway to the public endpoint. IAM least privilege on bedrock:InvokeModel is already in the design; this question is only the network path.
questions.question: Which network design keeps the Bedrock call on the AWS network?

options.text: A NAT Gateway so the private Lambda can reach the public Amazon Bedrock endpoint
An interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon Bedrock Runtime
A gateway VPC endpoint for Bedrock, using the same pattern the account already uses for Amazon S3
Amazon API Gateway with an AWS WAF web ACL in front of the public foundation-model URL

questions.explanation: Keep-filings-in-the-account is a 1.1 design constraint, not a later hardening ticket. Bedrock Runtime is reached through an interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink). Traffic stays on the AWS network. Gateway VPC endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB — they do not work for Bedrock. IAM on the caller is still required; the endpoint is the path, not the authorization.

incorrectExplanations.a: NAT lets the subnet reach the internet. The packet still leaves the VPC toward a public Bedrock endpoint. Legal asked for AWS-network-only.
incorrectExplanations.c: Gateway endpoints are the S3/DynamoDB pattern. Copying that onto Bedrock fails. Interface endpoint vs gateway endpoint is the exam fork.
incorrectExplanations.d: API Gateway plus WAF is a public HTTP front door (keys, throttles, authorizers). It does not keep the FM call on PrivateLink, and it does not replace a VPC endpoint for Runtime.

questions.scenario: The blotter must quote this quarter's NVDA 10-K and must never invent a revenue number. The filing changes every earnings morning. Two analysts must share the same corpus; pasting an 80-page exhibit into the prompt is not acceptable. The team is not trying to teach the model a house JSON schema or IR tone — only to ground answers in the exhibit. No custom weights for this requirement.
questions.question: Where should that knowledge live in the architecture?

options.text: Store the filings in Amazon S3 and retrieve them through an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base (RAG)
Fine-tune Amazon Titan on every historical 10-K so the facts are in the weights
Run continued pretraining on the full EDGAR dump so the model memorizes filings
Lengthen the system prompt with instructions to be accurate and never invent numbers

questions.explanation: Knowledge has three places: in the prompt (paste, demo-only), in a library the model consults (RAG), or in the weights (fine-tune / continued pretraining). Cite-the-exhibit and facts that change next week are RAG: S3 plus a Knowledge Base, Retrieve or RetrieveAndGenerate, citations from passages. Fine-tunes change behavior (format, tone). Weights have no footnote and go stale the day after the 8-K.

incorrectExplanations.b: A custom model can emit house JSON. It cannot cite this 10-K as a source, and it will not contain next quarter's numbers until you train again. The stem forbade custom weights and asked for quotes.
incorrectExplanations.c: Continued pretraining is domain adaptation from unlabeled text — still facts in weights, still no citation, still stale after earnings. Same trap as a fine-tune for knowledge.
incorrectExplanations.d: A constraint in the prompt is a behavioral instruction, not a corpus. Two people cannot share an 80-page filing that way, and "be accurate" does not ground the answer.

questions.scenario: Three IR desks each invented their own Lambda, logging, guardrail, and PrivateLink path. Leadership wants GenAI work aligned to AWS best practices and a path the next team can clone without rewriting those pieces. They are not asking for IDE completions, account-level Trusted Advisor tickets, or a shared notebook. Skill 1.1.3 is guidance plus standardized technical components.
questions.question: Which pair actually standardizes the design?

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor checks plus a wiki page of approved prompts
Amazon Q Developer enabled in every IDE so teams generate the same Lambda
One shared SageMaker notebook named platform that every desk opens
Well-Architected Generative AI Lens reviews plus a reusable IaC golden path (CDK or CloudFormation)

questions.explanation: Three different jobs: guidance is the Well-Architected Generative AI Lens (prompts, RAG, agents, non-deterministic output, token cost, prompt injection) run on a design. Standardization is reusable architecture modules — a golden path parameterized by model, Region, guardrail, logging, and app name. Enforcement is IAM, org-wide guardrail floor, VPC endpoints, SCPs. The Lens is a checklist, not a hosting service. The next desk clones the stack instead of inventing PrivateLink again.

incorrectExplanations.a: Trusted Advisor is account hygiene (idle resources, MFA). It does not review prompts, RAG, or token cost. A wiki is not a standardized technical component; the next squad still writes a new Lambda.
incorrectExplanations.b: Q Developer is the IDE/PR product (completions, reviews). It does not provision a company platform. Generating similar code is not an IaC golden path.
incorrectExplanations.c: A notebook is not a reusable, parameterized path. It does not give the next desk API Gateway, auth, Prompt Management, guardrail, and invocation logging as modules.

questions.scenario: The blotter path is always the same three steps: retrieve two 10-K exhibits from a Knowledge Base, summarize them, email IR. There are no extra tools, no SQL, no Jira, and no branching the model invents. Operations wants a graph they drew (and can version), not a ReAct loop that chooses actions. A person does not need to approve the email for this item.
questions.question: Which design matches a deterministic workflow?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents with several action groups so the model can choose tools
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows or AWS Step Functions — you specify the path
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, because every chatbot needs a production agent host
Fine-tune the foundation model so it memorizes retrieve → summarize → email as weights

questions.explanation: An agent is a behavior: the model decides which tool to call. That is not the same product as AgentCore, and it is not a workflow you already wrote down. When the steps are always retrieve → summarize → format (maybe Lambda), the design is Prompt Flows or Step Functions. Flows are the GenAI-centric graph (prompts, KB, Lambda, conditions, aliases). Step Functions is general AWS orchestration, retries, and later human-in-the-loop. You specify the path.

incorrectExplanations.a: Bedrock Agents are AWS-managed ReAct plus action groups. Use them when the model must choose among tools. A fixed three-step graph does not need ReAct; Agents add loop and ops you do not need.
incorrectExplanations.c: AgentCore hosts your agent code (Strands, LangGraph, CrewAI) with runtime, memory, identity, gateway, observability. This stem is not an agent. Do not reach for AgentCore because the word chatbot appeared.
incorrectExplanations.d: Do not bake a DAG into weights. Fine-tunes change format and tone. Orchestration belongs in Flows or Step Functions so you can version and roll back the graph.

questions.scenario: Easy blotter questions (ticker lookup, one-sentence recap) can use a small FM. Hard compares (NVDA vs AVGO across four transcripts) need the large sibling. Both models are in the same supported family. The goal is cost/quality at ask time. They are not trying to add quota for a single model ID, and they are not training a student model.
questions.question: Which lever picks the cheap or expensive writer at runtime?

options.text: Cross-Region inference on one model ID
Provisioned Throughput sized to the large model
Intelligent prompt routing across the small and large model (plus a fallback)
Distillation from the large model into the small one before Friday

questions.explanation: Three kinds of routing: CRI changes Region (same FM, capacity). Intelligent prompt routing changes Model in a family (easy → small, hard → large). Application routing is anything you put in AppConfig. Prompt routing chooses the cheaper model at runtime. Distillation trains the cheaper model to imitate the teacher beforehand.

incorrectExplanations.a: CRI is spare Regional capacity for the same writer. It does not pick easy vs hard prompts.
incorrectExplanations.b: Hourly MUs do not classify prompt difficulty. That is dedicated capacity.
incorrectExplanations.d: Distillation is the before-runtime cousin: teacher outputs train a student. The stem asked for a runtime pick, not a training job.

questions.scenario: Claude Sonnet writes excellent recaps. The desk wants a cheaper, faster student model that imitates those recaps before Friday’s traffic lands. They do not want a router that still calls Sonnet on hard prompts. The teacher will generate training responses onto S3; then a Bedrock or SageMaker job produces a custom student.
questions.question: Which customization is that?

options.text: Intelligent prompt routing between Sonnet and the small model at ask time
Cross-Region inference on Sonnet so it is cheaper
Distillation: teacher (Sonnet) generates responses; student trains to imitate them
Prompt caching on the 40k-token IR system prefix

questions.explanation: Distillation is the cost cousin of prompt routing. Routing picks the cheap model at ask time and may still call the teacher. Distillation trains the cheap model to imitate the teacher beforehand. You still deploy the custom student with Custom Model Deployment or PT. Caching discounts a repeated prefix; it does not create a smaller writer.

incorrectExplanations.a: Routing chooses; it does not train. Hard prompts would still hit Sonnet.
incorrectExplanations.b: CRI is capacity/resilience, same model, still Sonnet’s token price (plus geography). Not a student model.
incorrectExplanations.d: Prompt caching stores computed state of a supported repeated prefix. It does not cache completions and does not distill a student.

questions.scenario: The team evaluated three Bedrock FMs on 100 versioned analyst questions (their set, not a public leaderboard). Quality floor is ≥90% grounded accuracy. Latency is acceptable for all three. Nova Lite: 86% / $0.006 / 2.1 s. Claude Haiku: 91% / $0.009 / 2.5 s. Claude Sonnet: 95% / $0.041 / 5.8 s.
questions.question: Which model should they select?

options.text: Nova Lite, because it is the cheapest
Claude Haiku — the cheapest model that meets the quality floor
Claude Sonnet, because it has the highest accuracy and the largest context window in the brochure
All three behind intelligent prompt routing with no floor

questions.explanation: Skill 1.2.1: which model satisfies this workload’s quality floor at the lowest acceptable latency and cost — not which is smartest. Public leaderboards only narrow candidates. Nova Lite misses 90%. Haiku clears it and is the cheapest viable. Sonnet is better and maybe unnecessary. Routing is a later cost trick, not how you pick the primary.

incorrectExplanations.a: Cheapest fails the gate. Cost is evaluated after the floor, not instead of it.
incorrectExplanations.c: Highest accuracy is not the skill. You pay ~4× for a floor you already cleared. Brochures and leaderboards do not override your eval set.
incorrectExplanations.d: Prompt routing needs a supported family pair and still assumes you know the quality bar. It does not replace selecting a model that meets the floor.

questions.scenario: AWS Glue Data Quality flags a transcript file: revenue is null and the ticker column is missing. The next Step Functions state is Knowledge Base ingest. Product argues the blotter should still have *something* for NVDA this quarter. The DQ score is already published to CloudWatch.
questions.question: What should happen to that file?

options.text: Quarantine the record, emit a CloudWatch / SNS alarm, and do not ingest it
Ingest it anyway so retrieval has something, then fix the schema after analysts complain
Fine-tune the foundation model on the broken row so it learns to impute revenue
Raise temperature on Converse so the model fills the null at ask time

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.1: a validation workflow is inspect → pass or quarantine → alert. Glue Data Quality can identify failing records and publish passed / failed metrics to CloudWatch. An alarm on a DQ score below threshold stops the ingest. Do not silently drop garbage into the Knowledge Base.

incorrectExplanations.b: A null transcript that reaches retrieval becomes a fluent wrong answer. “Something” is not a quality rule. Quarantine is the point of the workflow.
incorrectExplanations.c: A broken schema is not a training problem. Fine-tuning does not repair a missing ticker column, and you do not train on quarantined junk.
incorrectExplanations.d: Sampling is not a schema repair. Temperature does not invent a complete filing.

questions.scenario: IR drops 50,000 10-K PDFs. They need company, revenue, tables, and a short summary as structured JSON — GenAI extraction, normalization, and structured output at document scale. They are not asking for OCR of a single form, for a similarity search over PDF bytes, or for a sensitive-data classifier.
questions.question: Which product matches the altitude of the job?

options.text: Amazon Textract on each PDF, then a homemade parser that maps lines into JSON
Amazon Bedrock Data Automation with a blueprint for the 10-K fields
Amazon Titan Text Embeddings invoked on the PDF bytes so fields fall out of the vector
Amazon Macie classification jobs over the bucket

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.2: Textract is OCR / forms / tables. Blueprint-driven multimodal understanding of piles of 10-Ks is Bedrock Data Automation. BDA can preserve paragraphs, figures, and tables and emit JSON / Markdown / HTML / CSV. Embeddings do not parse a PDF into fields.

incorrectExplanations.a: OCR is the wrong altitude for 50k structured 10-Ks. Textract is right when you need forms and tables from a scanned exhibit, not GenAI extraction at document scale.
incorrectExplanations.c: Text embedders do not take a PDF blob and emit company / revenue. That is a vector, not a schema.
incorrectExplanations.d: Macie finds sensitive data. It does not extract earnings JSON.

questions.scenario: Each S3 Put of a filing should map `NVIDIA Corporation` → `NVDA` in under a second before the object is copied to the curated prefix. There is no data lake job, no 500 GB corpus, and no analyst sitting in a visual prep UI. The map is deterministic: a known issuer name to a known ticker.
questions.question: Which kitchen is the fit?

options.text: An Amazon SageMaker Processing job that runs custom Python over the new object
A Glue ETL job over the data lake that rewrites issuer names in batch
A short AWS Lambda function invoked by the S3 event
SageMaker Data Wrangler as the production ingest path for every Put

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.1 / 1.3.4: four kitchens. A tiny deterministic map on an S3 event is Lambda (15-minute, event-shaped). Glue is production ETL around a lake. SageMaker Processing is your script at ML scale. Data Wrangler is interactive / little-code explore — flows can later feed production, but it is not this 200 ms map.

incorrectExplanations.a: Processing is managed compute for a 500 GB fine-tune corpus or a large eval set. It is the wrong kitchen for a ticker rewrite on Put.
incorrectExplanations.b: Glue is the lake: catalog, data quality, millions of rows. Not a sub-second event map.
incorrectExplanations.d: Wrangler is how analysts inspect a messy extract. It is not the production bell on every S3 Put.

questions.scenario: Turn 1 asked what NVDA said about Blackwell. Turn 2 is “Compare that with last quarter.” The Lambda stores nothing. The second Converse call sends only the new user sentence. The model asks which company. A teammate wants to switch to InvokeModel so the model will “keep the session.”
questions.question: What was missing?

options.text: Hidden session memory on the Bedrock model ID that Converse should have reused
A higher maxTokens cap so the model can recall the prior turn from its weights
Switching the call from Converse to InvokeModel, which keeps a server-side thread
A reconstructed messages array that includes the prior user and assistant turns, roles intact

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.3: the model does not remember the prior API call. Your app reconstructs the thread (DynamoDB, agent memory) and resends system + prior turns + the new user sentence on the next Converse request. Drop the history and “that” has nothing to point at.

incorrectExplanations.a: There is no hidden session on the model ID. Session storage is your job.
incorrectExplanations.b: maxTokens is output length. It is not memory of the last call.
incorrectExplanations.c: InvokeModel is the raw, model-specific JSON body. It also will not remember. Switching APIs is not a session store.

questions.scenario: Analyst notes already live as DynamoDB items (PK/SK, ticker, author, text). The desk wants similarity search beside that operational state, not an 80-million-vector cold archive.
questions.question: Which store fits?

options.text: Lambda scanning items and computing cosine in process
A DynamoDB vector index over embeddings on the items
Amazon S3 vector buckets as the system of record
Amazon Macie findings as the index

questions.explanation: DynamoDB vector indexes are for ANN beside data that already lives in the table. Lambda cosine is not an index. S3 Vectors is the infrequent archive.

incorrectExplanations.a: A scan is not k-NN.
incorrectExplanations.c: Wrong shelf: cheap/rare, not operational state.
incorrectExplanations.d: Discovery, not retrieval.

questions.scenario: The question is which suppliers are exposed to NVDA’s Blackwell ramp through CoWoS capacity — traversal of relationships, not “who sounded like Jensen.”
questions.question: Which engine belongs in the design?

options.text: S3 Vectors k-NN only
Neptune Analytics (GraphRAG: vectors plus graph traversal)
A DynamoDB table scan for supplier names
Amazon Comprehend syntax tokens

questions.explanation: Similar passages are vectors. Exposed-through-capacity is a graph. Neptune Analytics is the exam’s GraphRAG box.

incorrectExplanations.a: Neighbors that *sound* relevant, not a supply chain walk.
incorrectExplanations.c: No traversal.
incorrectExplanations.d: NLP, not a knowledge graph.

questions.scenario: Document A is tech-research only. Document B is healthcare only. A technology analyst asks what management is saying about AI demand.
questions.question: How should retrieval be constrained?

options.text: Search the whole corpus, then redact healthcare chunks in the prompt
Derive allowed groups from identity, apply a metadata filter, then run k-NN
Add “do not cite healthcare” to the system prompt
Lower topK so healthcare is statistically less likely

questions.explanation: Authorization constrains the search space. Do not retrieve B and hope the prompt stays quiet.

incorrectExplanations.a: You already retrieved the forbidden chunk.
incorrectExplanations.c: Instructions are not ACLs.
incorrectExplanations.d: Hope is not a filter.

questions.scenario: Small chunks hit the right NVDA sentence, but the FM answers without the surrounding section. Chunk size is otherwise fine.
questions.question: Which chunking change fits?

options.text: Hierarchical chunking: retrieve children, send parent context to the FM
Raise temperature so the model invents the missing paragraph
Move the index from OpenSearch to S3 Vectors
Disable overlap and keep only 50-token chunks

questions.explanation: Child embeddings retrieve precisely; parent text supplies context. Store swaps and sampling do not.

incorrectExplanations.b: Decoding is not chunking.
incorrectExplanations.c: Wrong shelf for a context-window problem.
incorrectExplanations.d: Makes the context problem worse.

questions.scenario: Analysts may only search NVDA, this quarter, earnings-call transcripts. SKU tokens like H100 still need a lexical match inside that set.
questions.question: What is the PRIMARY constraint, before hybrid ranking?

options.text: BM25 on the words “this quarter”
A metadata filter (ticker, quarter, document type), then search inside it
A larger embedding dimension
Prompt caching on the system prefix

questions.explanation: Filters define the room. Keyword and vectors rank what is relevant inside it. “This quarter” is not primarily BM25.

incorrectExplanations.a: Dates and tickers are hard predicates, not a hope that BM25 notices.
incorrectExplanations.c: Capacity of the vector, not the ACL/date room.
incorrectExplanations.d: Cost of a repeated prefix, not retrieval scope.

questions.scenario: The desk wants the top chunks, then it will build the prompt, call Converse, and attach citations itself. A managed one-shot answer is not required.
questions.question: Which Knowledge Base API?

options.text: RetrieveAndGenerate
Retrieve
InvokeModel with the entire 10-K in the body
Bedrock Batch Inference

questions.explanation: Retrieve returns evidence. RetrieveAndGenerate also writes the answer. Own the prompt → Retrieve.

incorrectExplanations.a: Managed answer + citations — more than they asked.
incorrectExplanations.c: Not retrieval.
incorrectExplanations.d: Offline JSONL, not a live retrieve.

questions.scenario: Legal reviews prompt graphs. Production must pin an immutable snapshot and roll back by repointing, not by editing a draft. They are using Bedrock Flows, not a lone Prompt Management template.
questions.question: What is the stable production pointer?

options.text: A Prompt Management `prod` alias
A Flow alias pointed at a published Flow version
A CloudTrail event selector named prod
The draft prompt, because drafts are live

questions.explanation: Prompt Management has versions, not a prod alias. Flows do: alias → version, then repoint to roll back.

incorrectExplanations.a: That alias does not exist on Prompt Management.
incorrectExplanations.c: Audit, not a pointer.
incorrectExplanations.d: Drafts are not production pins.

questions.scenario: The blotter sets temperature to 0 and still gets broken JSON and an invented `$27.0B` that is not in the exhibit.
questions.question: What is the reliable control?

options.text: Temperature 0 guarantees valid schema and factual numbers
Specify the schema in the prompt, then validate (and refuse) in Lambda
Raise top-k so the right brace is more likely
Disable stop sequences so the model can finish the JSON

questions.explanation: Temperature reduces sampling noise. It is not a fact control and not a schema guarantee. Validate.

incorrectExplanations.a: The trap the stem just demonstrated.
incorrectExplanations.c: Diversity knob.
incorrectExplanations.d: Stop sequences halt generation; they do not validate JSON.

questions.scenario: Compliance asks who invoked Converse last night, and also wants the prompt and completion bodies retained.
questions.question: Which pairing is correct?

options.text: CloudTrail for who called; invocation logging for the bodies
CloudTrail Lake, because it stores prompt text for seven years
Guardrail traces as the prompt archive
X-Ray annotations on the Lambda

questions.explanation: CloudTrail is API activity. Invocation logging (off by default) is the bodies to S3/CloudWatch. Do not confuse them.

incorrectExplanations.b: Trail is metadata, not the prompt/completion payload.
incorrectExplanations.c: Policy interventions, not a seven-year body store.
incorrectExplanations.d: Trace spans, not prompt WORM.

questions.scenario: A notebook converse() call returns a useful NVDA summary. Engineering wants the same prompt on the customer site this week. There is no eval set, no first-token or complete-answer budget, no cost cap per query, no adversarial safety test, and no measure of whether analysts accept the output. The API already returns HTTP 200.
questions.question: What is missing before this is a production design?

options.text: An Amazon EKS GPU cluster so the demo can scale if the site gets traffic
Provisioned Throughput, because any customer-facing traffic requires reserved Model Units
PoC exit gates for quality, latency, cost, safety, and business value — written thresholds, not only a working call
A fine-tune so the model memorizes last quarter's 10-K before go-live

questions.explanation: A successful API call does not prove a production design. Skill 1.1.2: a PoC should establish whether quality, latency, cost, safety, and business value meet minimum thresholds. Fail a gate → change the prompt, the model, the chunks, or kill the idea. Do not add API Gateway and Provisioned Throughput to a demo analysts will not use. The numbers on the curriculum page are examples; the exam cares that you have thresholds.

incorrectExplanations.a: EKS is a later, heavier runtime. Scaling infrastructure does not replace quality, cost, or safety gates. The stem has no evidence the idea even works for analysts.
incorrectExplanations.b: Provisioned Throughput is hourly Model Units for steady dedicated capacity (or some custom models). Spiky or unproven customer traffic is still on-demand or CRI. Reserved MUs are not the missing design artifact.
incorrectExplanations.d: Last quarter's 10-K belongs in a Knowledge Base if you need citations. Memorizing it in weights is the wrong knowledge store and does not define production gates.

questions.scenario: The desk already has a LangGraph agent in Python. It must return a sub-second ticker JSON for "what did NVDA print?" and stream a multi-minute NVDA vs AVGO compare. The team wants production hosting, memory, identity, tool connectivity, and observability with minimal new infrastructure. They are not starting from a blank ReAct agent that AWS should run for them. The stem names Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime as the destination.
questions.question: Which box should the design pick?

options.text: Rewrite the loop as Amazon Bedrock Agents with action groups so AWS owns ReAct
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate with a hand-rolled FastAPI /invocations and /ping server
Amazon SageMaker real-time inference with a custom container, because it also exposes /invocations and /ping
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (existing Python on Runtime) — not a rewrite into action groups

questions.explanation: Need the model to decide tools → an agent. Already wrote Strands/LangGraph/CrewAI and need production hosting → AgentCore, not ECS first. Bedrock Agents is AWS-managed ReAct plus a few Lambdas when you have little code. AgentCore is the platform for your agent. Same-looking /invocations paths on ECS or SageMaker are different products. Implementation of SDK vs starter toolkit is task 2.1; 1.1 only has to pick the box.

incorrectExplanations.a: Bedrock Agents would throw away the existing LangGraph loop. Use Agents when AWS should run ReAct for you with KB plus a few Lambdas. The stem already has Python and named AgentCore Runtime.
incorrectExplanations.b: Fargate means you do not patch EC2. You still own images, task definitions, the HTTP contract, and health. The design asked for the AgentCore host, not containers you run.
incorrectExplanations.c: SageMaker real-time /invocations is a model endpoint contract (task 2.2), not an agent runtime. Same path names, different restaurant.

questions.scenario: Employees need to ask "What is our travel policy?" over SharePoint and internal wikis. Answers must honor each user's existing document ACLs — a researcher must not see HR-only files. The company does not need custom tools, Jira, or SQL. They would rather not design a Bedrock Agent, a Knowledge Base, and a homemade authorizer to reconstruct badge-aware retrieval.
questions.question: Which product is the feature?

options.text: Amazon Q Business — employee chat over company data with identity-aware ACLs
Amazon Q Developer in the IDE, pointed at the SharePoint tenant
A homemade Amazon Bedrock Agent with a Knowledge Base and a custom ACL filter you maintain
Amazon QuickSight natural-language queries over a travel-policy dashboard

questions.explanation: Do not build Bedrock when a prebuilt product is the feature. Q Business is employee chat over company docs (SharePoint, wikis) with identity-aware ACLs. Q Developer is code in the IDE/PRs. A homemade agent can be built; the stem asked for the product that already is the feature. QuickSight is BI over dashboards, not a policy wiki.

incorrectExplanations.b: Two different Qs. Q Developer sits in the IDE, CLI, and PRs (completions, reviews). It does not replace badge-aware enterprise chat over SharePoint.
incorrectExplanations.c: You can assemble Agents + KB + filters. Task 1.1 says pick the prebuilt box when that box is the requirement. Homemade ACL retrieval is extra ops the stem wanted to avoid.
incorrectExplanations.d: QuickSight (Amazon Quick) is natural-language questions over metrics and charts. Travel policy in SharePoint is not a dashboard.

questions.scenario: Traders will stare at the blotter. A 12-second blank spinner until the full completion returns is not acceptable. The same Claude model is fine. Callers are internal users through a browser, not a nightly file of prompts. The team must pick how the request reaches the model: latency and who is calling, not which FM.
questions.question: Which pipe paints tokens as they generate?

options.text: Synchronous REST request/response through API Gateway that waits for the whole completion
converse_stream (or InvokeModelWithResponseStream) plus API Gateway WebSocket or SSE
Amazon SQS so each question becomes a queued job the trader polls
Amazon Bedrock Batch Inference over a JSONL file of trader questions

questions.explanation: Same FM, different pipes. Streaming: the model emits tokens as it generates; WebSocket or SSE paints the caret. REST request/response waits for the whole completion. Event-driven SQS/EventBridge is for work that can finish later. Batch Inference is JSONL in, JSONL out, hours, cheapest tokens — not a chatbot. Do not put a chat UI on SQS.

incorrectExplanations.a: Production HTTP with keys and throttles is the usual front door, but a single request/response still holds the spinner until the last token. The stem's latency constraint is tokens on screen.
incorrectExplanations.c: SQS is the event-driven pipe: 10-K lands, worker calls Bedrock, result to S3/DynamoDB. Traders will not poll a queue for a live answer.
incorrectExplanations.d: Batch is overnight recaps and 10k tickets. It is the managed cheaper cousin of a live queue, not an interactive blotter.

questions.scenario: The blotter is quiet overnight and spikes for about three hours on NVDA print morning. The design must name the traffic shape now, even if day-one config is still on-demand. Compliance requires the same foundation model; they will not swap to a cheaper sibling at the peak. They do not want to pay for idle Model Units at 3 a.m. Custom models are not in scope.
questions.question: Which capacity shape fits a burst of the same FM?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput sized to the print-morning peak, left running all month
Intelligent prompt routing to a smaller model in the family during the spike
Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoints autoscale because Bedrock cannot absorb a spike
On-demand with cross-Region inference (a geographic inference profile) if the Region hits Too many requests

questions.explanation: At design time, name the shape: on-demand (shared quota, PoC and spiky, can 429), CRI (same FM, other Region in the geography, still token-priced), PT (hourly MUs, flat 24/7 or dedicated custom capacity), Custom Model Deployment (supported custom, on-demand tokens), batch (hours). A three-hour earnings spike is CRI or a bigger on-demand quota, not a month of idle MUs. Custom models cannot use CRI. Prompt routing changes which model answers — the stem forbade that.

incorrectExplanations.a: PT is the right shape for predictable high utilization. Paying peak MUs through the night is the wrong bill. You did not graduate to SageMaker by buying PT; PT is still Bedrock.
incorrectExplanations.b: Intelligent prompt routing is easy vs hard prompts, same family, cost/quality at runtime. It is not extra quota for one FM, and it violates "same model."
incorrectExplanations.c: Staying on Bedrock is the 1.1.1 default. CRI is Bedrock's peak relief. SageMaker is for a training loop or a runtime Bedrock will not host.

questions.scenario: A partner drops a 50 MB research pack. Parsing on GPU takes about 12 minutes. Interactive chat is not required; the user can wait for a callback. Amazon Bedrock Converse payload and timeout limits will not run this job. The team does not have an existing GPU runtime that only EKS can host — they need a managed box they size.
questions.question: When does the design leave Bedrock for SageMaker?

options.text: Synchronous Lambda invoking Bedrock Converse with the 50 MB pack in the prompt
Amazon EKS with DJL Serving as the first choice, before considering SageMaker
Amazon SageMaker asynchronous inference on an accelerated instance
Amazon Bedrock Batch Inference, because every long job is a JSONL batch

questions.explanation: Bedrock vs SageMaker vs EKS is the 1.1.1 fork. Bedrock is the managed FM API. SageMaker is the box you size: training, real-time or async endpoints, JumpStart, custom DJL/vLLM, Inferentia — when you need a training loop, a GPU you tune, a model Bedrock does not host, or a long/large-file job Bedrock will not run. Large payload plus minutes-long GPU work is SageMaker async. EKS only if Bedrock and SageMaker refuse the runtime.

incorrectExplanations.a: Do not run a 50 MB, 15-minute GPU job on synchronous Lambda or a Bedrock chat call. Payload, timeout, and the wrong host all fail.
incorrectExplanations.b: EKS is last. The stem said they do not already have a runtime only EKS can run. SageMaker async is the managed box.
incorrectExplanations.d: Bedrock Batch Inference is cheap overnight JSONL for FM prompts. It is not a 50 MB custom GPU parse with a per-user callback.

questions.scenario: The graph is retrieve exhibits → summarize → email IR. Compliance now requires a person to approve the email before it sends. The path is still deterministic; the model does not choose extra tools. The pause must be a first-class state, not a hope that the FM waits.
questions.question: Which product owns a human-in-the-loop side effect?

options.text: AWS Step Functions with a human-in-the-loop pause, then the email task
A system prompt that says "ask IR before emailing" and trust the model to stop
Amazon Bedrock Agents so the model can decide whether to email
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, which is the Cognito login for the analyst

questions.explanation: A person must approve a side effect → Step Functions human-in-the-loop. The steps are still ones you specified. Prompt Flows remain the GenAI graph when you do not need that AWS-wide wait/approval machinery. Instructions in the prompt are not a control. AgentCore Identity is credentials for the agent to call AWS and third parties — not a Cognito login screen for a human.

incorrectExplanations.b: Behavioral instructions are not an approval workflow. The model can ignore them. Orchestration must pause.
incorrectExplanations.c: Agents are for when the model chooses tools. Compliance asked for a required human gate, not optional ReAct.
incorrectExplanations.d: AgentCore Identity is agent-to-system credentials. Analyst sign-in is Cognito or IAM Identity Center (task 2.3). Wrong identity, wrong layer.

questions.scenario: The desk must not give investment advice and must not echo SSNs from a pasted exhibit. Security wants a named policy evaluated on the way in and the way out of the same Converse call. They do not want a homemade moderator Lambda in front of the SDK as the primary control. Prompt text that says "please never recommend a stock" may still exist, but it is not the boundary.
questions.question: How should the design attach that control?

options.text: A longer system prompt only — instructions are the security boundary
A Bedrock Guardrail on the Converse call (guardrailConfig), not a wrapper proxy as the enforcement
A Lambda that regex-scans the prompt, then calls Converse without a guardrail
Amazon Macie on the Knowledge Base index as the denied-topic filter

questions.explanation: A guardrail is a named policy (denied topics, PII, prompt-attack filters) evaluated on input and output. Attach it on Converse; do not wrap the SDK in a homemade moderator first. "Do not give investment recommendations" in the system prompt is a behavioral instruction. The Guardrail is the control. Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it is not the live I/O filter. Detail of traces and IAM conditions is domain 3; 1.1 only picks the box on the same call.

incorrectExplanations.a: Instructions can be bypassed and are not evaluated as a named policy on input and output. Keep them if they help; they are not the boundary.
incorrectExplanations.c: A proxy that injects checks is extra ops and still not the Bedrock-native policy. IAM can later require a GuardrailIdentifier; a regex Lambda does not replace that.
incorrectExplanations.d: Macie classifies sensitive objects in S3. It does not attach a denied-topic or PII policy to Converse.

questions.scenario: Three analysts in a notebook is over. The blotter must be a customer-facing HTTPS API: API keys, usage plans, WAF, a Cognito authorizer, and throttles at the edge. The public URL must stay stable while the team swaps model IDs. Inference remains Amazon Bedrock Converse from Lambda. This is who is calling, not which FM.
questions.question: Which front door is the usual production HTTP shape?

options.text: A laptop or notebook calling Converse directly, because that is how the PoC worked
Amazon SQS as the public URL so customers enqueue questions
Amazon API Gateway → Lambda → Bedrock Runtime, with keys, authorizer, and throttles on the gateway
Move the foundation model onto Amazon SageMaker so API Gateway can target an endpoint

questions.explanation: Direct Lambda → Bedrock is right for the PoC and an internal tool you control; you own retries, throttling, and the external contract. Production users → API Gateway → Lambda → Bedrock. The URL stays stable while you swap models (AppConfig lives in 1.2). Streaming would add WebSocket; this stem is the HTTP shape. You did not graduate to SageMaker because you added a front door.

incorrectExplanations.a: Direct is the PoC pipe. Customer keys, WAF, and a stable URL are the gateway's job.
incorrectExplanations.b: SQS is event-driven work that can finish later. It is not a customer HTTPS contract with usage plans.
incorrectExplanations.d: The FM can stay on Bedrock. API Gateway in front of Lambda does not require a SageMaker endpoint.

questions.scenario: Two requirements, not one. (1) Every answer must cite this quarter's NVDA 10-K; numbers change every earnings morning. (2) The completion must always be house JSON (current_quarter, prior_quarter, change, citations) in IR tone. The team already knows a prompt-plus-validator might be enough for JSON, but leadership asked for the architecture pair when they are willing to customize behavior and keep facts out of the weights.
questions.question: Which TWO stores match those two jobs? (Select TWO)

options.text: Continued pretraining on the 10-Ks so citations come from the weights
A Knowledge Base over the 10-Ks for the facts and citations
Amazon EKS plus DJL Serving so both facts and format live in the cluster
A fine-tune (then Custom Model Deployment or Provisioned Throughput) for house JSON and tone

questions.explanation: Facts that change and must be cited → RAG (Knowledge Base). House JSON / tone when you are customizing behavior → fine-tune, then invoke with Custom Model Deployment or PT. Still retrieve the exhibit; the custom model is not a fourth knowledge store. An agent is a behavior that uses a KB. A bigger prompt is not an agent and is not a substitute for the filing.

incorrectExplanations.a: Continued pretraining puts domain text in the weights. Weights have no footnote and go stale. That is the wrong store for "cite this 10-K."
incorrectExplanations.c: EKS is a runtime, not a knowledge store. You still have to choose RAG vs weights. Do not start a cluster to hold either job.

questions.scenario: Engineering shortlisted three Bedrock FMs from a public leaderboard: all three support Converse, the Region, and the context window the 10-K plus history will need. Product wants to “just take #1 on the board.” There is no in-house prompt dataset yet.
questions.question: What is still required before they pick?

options.text: Nothing — the public leaderboard is sufficient once modality and Region match
Evaluate the candidates on their own versioned analyst questions for quality, latency, cost, and safety
Buy Provisioned Throughput on the leaderboard winner so the pick is official
Fine-tune all three and choose whichever custom model trains

questions.explanation: Leaderboards narrow the shortlist (modality, window, Region, features). Your 50–100 analyst questions pick the winner. Bedrock Model Evaluations (automatic / human / LLM-as-judge) score quality, latency, cost, and safety on that set. You do not choose an FM from a leaderboard alone.

incorrectExplanations.a: Catalog fit is necessary, not sufficient. Task quality is performance on your eval set.
incorrectExplanations.c: PT is a capacity SKU after you know which model. It does not validate the pick.
incorrectExplanations.d: Customization is later (1.2.4), and only if behavior — not the catalog choice — needs it. Do not fine-tune to avoid an eval.

questions.scenario: The blotter uses Converse, so the message shape is the same across providers. A teammate wants to swap the AppConfig modelId from Claude to Nova on Friday and skip eval because “Converse already standardized the API.” Context windows, tool support, and inference parameters differ between the two models.
questions.question: What is the trap?

options.text: Converse forbids changing modelId without a new IAM role
Nova cannot be stored in AppConfig
They must move off Converse to InvokeModel before any swap
Converse standardizes the request envelope, not capabilities — re-run the same eval set after the swap

questions.explanation: Converse helps because the message shape is the same across providers. It does not make every model identical. Context windows, modalities, tool support, inference parameters, Regions, and Bedrock feature compatibility still differ. Blindly swapping IDs is an exam trap: you still test the candidate on the same eval set.

incorrectExplanations.a: IAM must allow the new model, but that is not why you re-eval. The trap is capability drift, not a hidden role requirement.
incorrectExplanations.b: AppConfig can hold any modelId string. Storage is not the issue.
incorrectExplanations.c: InvokeModel is the older model-specific JSON body. Switching to it does not fix a blind swap and is the wrong direction.

questions.scenario: A fine-tuned blotter model must run 24/7 at a predictable QPS. Custom Model Deployment is not offered for this model/Region. The team asked for cross-Region inference “like the base FM” to save money at night. Legal still requires this custom artifact, not the base catalog ID.
questions.question: How is this custom model hosted?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput (Model Units by the hour) — CRI is not available on custom models
A us. inference profile pointed at the custom model ID
Shared on-demand with the base FM ID; Bedrock will find the fine-tune
Intelligent prompt routing between the custom model and Haiku

questions.explanation: Custom FM paths: on-demand Custom Model Deployment where supported, otherwise Provisioned Throughput. Custom models cannot use CRI. This stem shut the CMD door and asked for dedicated predictable capacity — that is PT. Base-FM on-demand will not serve your artifact.

incorrectExplanations.b: Inference profiles are for on-demand foundation models. Custom artifacts do not ride CRI.
incorrectExplanations.c: The catalog ID is the base model. Your fine-tune is a different artifact that must be deployed (CMD or PT).
incorrectExplanations.d: Routing is a runtime pick among supported family FMs, not a hosting mode for a custom model that has no CMD.

questions.scenario: The IR methodology block is about 40k tokens and barely changes. Each analyst question is a few hundred tokens. Token cost is dominated by re-processing that prefix on every Converse call. Completions are unique; they do not want to serve yesterday’s answer. The model supports prompt caching.
questions.question: Which lever fits FIRST?

options.text: Cache the completion in DynamoDB and skip Bedrock on repeat tickers
Provisioned Throughput sized to overnight idle
Bedrock prompt caching on the stable prefix so later calls skip re-processing those input tokens
Raise temperature so answers are shorter

questions.explanation: Prompt caching stores the computed state of a supported, repeated prefix. Later calls skip re-processing those input tokens — cheaper, often faster. It does not cache the completion. A unique 8k retrieved blob with nothing shared will not help. Deeper cost treatment is task 4.1; 1.2 still names the lever at design time.

incorrectExplanations.a: That is an answer cache. The stem said completions are unique and they do not want yesterday’s recap. Caching the prefix is the coat check, not the leftover plate.
incorrectExplanations.b: Wrong bill shape. PT does not shrink the repeated prefix.
incorrectExplanations.d: Temperature is not a cost control and may worsen quality.

questions.scenario: A single Converse call returns a transient 429. The primary model is healthy overall; this is a blip, not a dead Region or a model that returns garbage. The team has CRI, a circuit breaker, a fallback model, and a cached summary ready, but they must not skip the first step.
questions.question: What is the FIRST response?

options.text: Open the circuit breaker and stop sending traffic
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
Immediately switch to the fallback model in AppConfig
Return last night’s cached summary and skip the FM

questions.explanation: Failure is not one thing (skill 1.2.3). Stack the responses: transient 429/5xx → retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Capacity pressure → CRI (same FM). Repeated failure → circuit breaker (stop hammering). Model/provider down → fallback model. Entire path dead → cached or degraded response. A circuit breaker sits in front of CRI; it does not replace CRI. Do not pick one lever and stop.

incorrectExplanations.a: The breaker is for repeated failure (CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN). One blip is not that. Opening it now drops good traffic.
incorrectExplanations.c: Fallback is when the primary is gone (Sonnet unavailable → Haiku). A single 429 is still the same writer after a wait.
incorrectExplanations.d: Graceful degradation is the last rung, when generation is unavailable. The UI should not go blank — but you have not exhausted retry or CRI yet.

questions.scenario: The failover path is already written down: invoke primary; on transient 429 retry with backoff; still failing, invoke the AppConfig fallback model; still failing, return retrieved 10-K passages only. The model does not need to choose tools. Ops wants a deterministic state machine, not ReAct.
questions.question: Which product should own that path?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents so the model can decide when to retry
AgentCore Runtime, because failover is an agent behavior
AWS Step Functions (invoke → retry → fallback → degrade)
A circuit breaker alone, with no CRI and no fallback

questions.explanation: Skill 1.2.3 names Step Functions for a path you already wrote down. You do not need an agent to decide “if the API fails three times, call backup.” That is a deterministic workflow. Agents are for when the model must choose tools. A breaker without CRI or fallback is only one rung of the stack.

incorrectExplanations.a: ReAct choosing retries is overkill and non-deterministic. The stem already specified the graph.
incorrectExplanations.b: AgentCore hosts your agent code. This is not an agent. Wrong box.
incorrectExplanations.d: A circuit breaker sits in front of CRI and stops hammering. It does not replace CRI, fallback, or a degraded response.

questions.scenario: Facts already live in a Knowledge Base. The team wants the model to write house JSON from labeled examples (supervised). Separately, research asks about a different job: they have an objective grader (relevance / faithfulness scores) and want to optimize against that reward, not a fixed JSONL of input-output pairs.
questions.question: Which customization matches the grader/reward job?

options.text: Continued pretraining on unlabeled 10-K text to “add this week’s filing”
Supervised fine-tuning on the JSON examples — it is the same job
Intelligent prompt routing, which trains the small model on the grader
Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) against the reward / grader

questions.explanation: RAG changes what the model knows at inference time. Customization changes how it behaves. Supervised fine-tuning is labeled examples (the JSON job). RFT is when you have an objective reward/grader. Continued pretraining is domain adaptation from unlabeled text — it does not cite this week’s 10-K. Distillation/LoRA are other rows. Do not fine-tune to add a filing.

incorrectExplanations.a: Unlabeled domain adaptation, and the wrong store for a changing 10-K. Put the filing in the Knowledge Base.
incorrectExplanations.b: SFT is the JSON-examples job. The grader/reward job is RFT. They are not the same.
incorrectExplanations.c: Prompt routing picks a model at runtime. It does not train against a reward.

questions.scenario: A new custom blotter model (v3) beat v2 on the offline eval and was approved. Production still points at v2. The team must send a small slice of live traffic to v3, watch quality and error metrics, and be able to reverse the cutover without editing 17 Lambdas. SageMaker Model Registry already versions the package.
questions.question: What completes a reversible release?

options.text: Hardcode MODEL=v3 in every Lambda and redeploy if it fails
Replace v2 immediately with 100% traffic because offline eval passed
Delete v2 from the registry so only v3 can answer
Canary or blue/green (for example 5% → 25% → 100%) with CloudWatch alarms that roll back to v2; keep the production pointer in AppConfig / the registry

questions.explanation: Skill 1.2.4 is the lifecycle, not a one-shot job: customize → evaluate → Model Registry → approval → canary/blue-green → production → monitor → rollback / replace / retire. Registry versions the package, keeps lineage and approval states, and plugs into CI/CD. “Version it so you can roll back” is the minimum. AWS wants the deploy to be reversible. AppConfig and the registry are the pointer; not MODEL in 17 Lambdas.

incorrectExplanations.a: That is the anti-pattern the curriculum names. A failed release then needs 17 deploys to undo.
incorrectExplanations.b: Offline eval is the gate to a candidate, not to 100% live traffic. Canary on live metrics next.
incorrectExplanations.c: Retire v2 after v3 is healthy. Deleting the rollback target is the opposite of reversible.
