questions.scenario: The production Bedrock FM is moving Active → Legacy → EOL. Customization options shrink once a model is Legacy. The blotter’s modelId is already in AppConfig. The replacement candidate is in the same Region and passes a first look at modality.
questions.question: What does AWS expect before retirement?

options.text: Keep calling the Legacy ID until it 404s, then hardcode a new one
Fine-tune the Legacy model so EOL does not apply to custom artifacts
Evaluate a replacement on the same dataset and cut the AppConfig pointer over to an Active model
Buy Provisioned Throughput on the Legacy model to freeze it past EOL

questions.explanation: Bedrock FMs move Active → Legacy → EOL. AWS expects you to migrate workloads to Active models before retirement. Treat the production pointer as a config alias, evaluate a replacement on the same dataset, and cut over. Customization options can shrink on Legacy. PT does not extend EOL.

incorrectExplanations.a: Waiting for a hard failure is not a migration. The pointer should move while you still have time to eval.
incorrectExplanations.b: A custom artifact on a retiring base does not exempt you from EOL. You still migrate.
incorrectExplanations.d: Reserved capacity does not stop a model family from retiring. Wrong lever.

questions.scenario: The team wants parameter-efficient adaptation: a thin extra matrix, not a full-weight fine-tune, then the same custom-artifact deploy path. They already know RAG holds the 10-Ks. This is not distillation (no teacher dump) and not RFT (no grader).
questions.question: Which customization matches?

options.text: LoRA / adapters, then Custom Model Deployment or Provisioned Throughput
Continued pretraining on this week’s 10-K so the adapter contains the filing
Intelligent prompt routing, which is an adapter at runtime
Prompt caching, which trains a prefix adapter

questions.explanation: LoRA / adapters train a thin extra matrix instead of all weights. Same lifecycle as other custom artifacts: job on S3 JSONL → custom model → Custom Model Deployment or PT. It still does not put this week’s 10-K in the weights.

incorrectExplanations.b: Continued pretraining is unlabeled domain adaptation, and filings belong in a Knowledge Base. An adapter is not a RAG substitute.
incorrectExplanations.c: Prompt routing picks among catalog FMs at ask time. It is not a trained adapter.
incorrectExplanations.d: Caching is a prefix discount on supported models. It does not train weights.

questions.scenario: The earnings lake already lives in the Glue Data Catalog: millions of filing rows, nightly ETL. Before those rows reach a foundation model, the team must enforce completeness, uniqueness, and type with rules the ETL job evaluates automatically. They want a data quality score in CloudWatch, not a new Lambda for every check. Analysts are not sitting in a visual prep UI.
questions.question: Which approach matches the stem?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Quality with a DQDL ruleset that returns a score and publishes passed / failed metrics to CloudWatch
A fleet of Lambda functions with if/else checks on each row, because validation must be imperative
SageMaker Data Wrangler as the production quality gate on every nightly job
Amazon Comprehend entity detection, which is how AWS scores tabular completeness

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.1: Glue Data Quality runs declarative DQDL checks on the catalog and in ETL, identifies failing records, and publishes passed / failed metrics to CloudWatch. A ruleset is a list of checks (ColumnExists, IsComplete, IsUnique). That is the lake kitchen, not a homemade validator.

incorrectExplanations.b: Lambda is the right kitchen for a tiny event-shaped map, not for declarative lake rules. Imperative if/else is what DQDL is meant to replace on cataloged ETL.
incorrectExplanations.c: Wrangler is interactive explore / prepare. Flows can later feed production; it is not the automated DQ score on a nightly Glue job.
incorrectExplanations.d: Comprehend is NLP enrichment (entities, sentiment, PII). It does not evaluate a tabular DQDL ruleset.

questions.scenario: The desk will fine-tune a Bedrock custom model. Training JSONL is 500 GB of labeled analyst notes on S3. The preprocess is custom Python (normalize speakers, drop boilerplate, emit JSONL). This is not an S3-event ticker rewrite, not a visual explore of a sample extract, and not cataloged lake ETL with DQDL.
questions.question: Which kitchen runs that preprocess?

options.text: A 15-minute Lambda on each Put of a note, because all transforms are Lambdas
SageMaker Data Wrangler, because any training-set prep is Wrangler
Glue Data Quality alone, because a DQ score is the preprocess
A SageMaker Processing job that runs the custom Python / container at ML scale

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.1: SageMaker Processing is managed compute when the script is yours and the volume is large — a 500 GB fine-tune corpus or a post-job eval set. Fine-tuning JSONL is one use of Processing, not the definition of Lambda, Glue, or Wrangler.

incorrectExplanations.a: Lambda is the 15-minute event-shaped cousin. 500 GB will time out and is the wrong scale.
incorrectExplanations.b: Wrangler is interactive / little-code. It can later feed production; it is not “the training-set kitchen” by default.
incorrectExplanations.c: Glue Data Quality validates. It does not run your 500 GB speaker-normalize script.

questions.scenario: Two analysts received a messy vendor extract of 12,000 rows: mixed date formats, issuer names, and null sectors. They need to inspect, clean, and featurize it in a visual flow this afternoon. The flow should be reusable later; they are not writing a Spark job today and they are not mapping a single S3 Put.
questions.question: Which kitchen fits the explore step?

options.text: SageMaker Processing as the first click, because any Data Wrangler work must start as a cluster job
A production Glue ETL job they cannot see, because lakes forbid interactive prep
SageMaker Data Wrangler for interactive / little-code prepare; the flow can later feed production
Amazon Textract, because messy tables are always OCR

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.1: Data Wrangler is the visual / interactive path. Its flows can feed production; it is not only a one-off training set, and it is not the 200 ms S3-event map. Processing is the later scale-out of a script you already wrote.

incorrectExplanations.a: Processing is custom Python / Spark / container at ML scale after you know the recipe. Do not start there for a 12k-row inspect.
incorrectExplanations.b: Glue is the lake kitchen for production ETL and data quality. It is not how two analysts explore a messy extract this afternoon.
incorrectExplanations.d: Textract is OCR / forms / tables on documents. A vendor CSV is not a scanned 10-K.

questions.scenario: Product wants semantic search across NVDA webcast audio itself — “clips that sound like this supply-constraint remark” — using Nova Multimodal Embeddings. They do not need an exact searchable transcript, and they are not asking for a BDA blob of transcript + summary + metadata. A teammate still wants Transcribe first “because audio always becomes text.”
questions.question: What does the downstream model require?

options.text: A multimodal embedding pipeline on the audio in native form — do not force it through text first
Amazon Transcribe, then Titan Text Embeddings, because Knowledge Bases cannot touch audio
Bedrock Data Automation as the only legal path for any MP3 on S3
Amazon Polly, which converts speech to a format Titan Text Embeddings will accept

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.2: incoming data is not automatically “make it text.” Knowledge Bases can work with images, audio, and video. Nova Multimodal Embeddings can embed multimedia natively. Transcribe is the path when you need an exact searchable transcript for a text embedder.

incorrectExplanations.b: Knowledge Bases can work with audio. Transcribe-then-text-embed is the passage-search job (xd-21), which this stem explicitly is not.
incorrectExplanations.c: BDA turns media into text or structured JSON when you want transcript + summaries + metadata in one blob. It is a third path, not the only MP3 path.
incorrectExplanations.d: Polly is text-to-speech. It does not embed webcasts.

questions.scenario: Legal scans a single NVDA exhibit: a checked-box 8-K form with a table of share counts. They need OCR of those forms and tables as text, not a 50,000-document GenAI JSON blueprint, and not a multimodal FM “looking” at the page to write a paragraph. The downstream model is a text FM.
questions.question: Which processing path matches?

options.text: Bedrock Data Automation over the whole IR corpus, because every PDF is BDA
Send the scan as an image on Converse and skip extraction, because the text FM will OCR it
Amazon Textract to extract text and tables, then enhance and format for the text FM
Amazon Rekognition celebrity detection, which reads form checkboxes

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.2: OCR / forms / tables is Textract. A multimodal FM looking at the exhibit is a different path. Blueprint-driven extraction of piles of 10-Ks is BDA. Same PDF, three products — pick from the job.

incorrectExplanations.a: BDA is the right altitude for 50k 10-Ks into structured JSON. A single scanned form with checkboxes is Textract.
incorrectExplanations.b: A text FM does not replace OCR. If you wanted the model to look, you would use a multimodal Converse / Knowledge Base path, which this stem forbade.
incorrectExplanations.d: Rekognition is image/video analysis, not form OCR.

questions.scenario: A Glue table of fundamentals has 400 columns. The blotter must ask a text FM “how did NVDA’s data-center revenue move vs last year?” using a handful of those columns. The table already passed Glue Data Quality. A developer wants to stringify the entire row into the Converse prompt “so the model has everything.”
questions.question: What does the pipeline still owe the model?

options.text: Nothing — dataset-valid means the row is already a valid model request
Fine-tune Titan on the 400-column dump so the weights absorb the schema
Amazon Kendra, because tabular lakes cannot be serialized for Bedrock
Project the relevant columns, normalize units and nulls, and serialize a JSON fragment or markdown table the FM can consume

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.2 / 1.3.3: tabular path is validate schema → normalize → select rows / columns → serialize into a representation the model can consume. Dataset-valid is not request-valid. Do not paste a 400-column dump into Converse and hope.

incorrectExplanations.a: Glue DQ passing means the lake row is complete. The FM still needs a mapped, sized payload. That is 1.3.1 meeting 1.3.3.
incorrectExplanations.b: Fine-tuning does not make a 400-column paste a good prompt, and it is the wrong store for facts that already live in Glue.
incorrectExplanations.c: Kendra is enterprise search, not the serializer. Tabular lakes routinely become JSON or markdown for Converse.

questions.scenario: The blotter still calls InvokeModel for a Titan Text G1 request. Anthropic’s Claude body on the same account uses a different JSON shape. A Lambda already cleaned the filing text. Calls fail with a 400 even though Glue DQ passed. A teammate says Converse would erase Titan’s knobs so they should keep concatenating a string that looks like Claude’s body.
questions.question: What does skill 1.3.3 require?

options.text: Stop validating the lake, because a 400 always means the transcript was null
Map the cleaned filing into Titan’s request body (inputText / textGenerationConfig) — Converse standardizes the envelope, not every model’s knobs
Send the Glue table bytes on the wire; InvokeModel will infer the schema
Switch the modelId to Claude without changing the body, because Bedrock rewrites vendor JSON

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.3: after cleaning, map to the contract the API wants. InvokeModel is the raw, model-specific JSON — Anthropic’s body is not Titan’s. A small Lambda that maps “filing → request body” is the adapter. Converse is the provider-neutral envelope; model-specific knobs still go in additionalModelRequestFields. A 400 that looks like a model failure is often a body you never mapped.

incorrectExplanations.a: DQ passing is why this is a formatting bug, not a quarantine bug. Do not skip validation because the API returned 400.
incorrectExplanations.c: SageMaker endpoints have their own serializer; Bedrock InvokeModel also wants a named JSON body, not a table dump.
incorrectExplanations.d: Bedrock does not rewrite a Claude-shaped body into Titan. That is the adapter you write.

questions.scenario: A custom scoring model is hosted on a SageMaker real-time endpoint. The container’s /invocations contract wants a JSON lines body with named float fields. The app currently dumps the Converse messages array at the endpoint and gets 415 / 400. The team wants “Bedrock formatting” applied unchanged.
questions.question: What is the missing step?

options.text: Serialize to the container’s structured /invocations contract — SageMaker is not the Converse envelope
Wrap the SageMaker call in Converse so messages[] becomes universal
Put the endpoint ARN in AppConfig and skip serialization, because aliases format payloads
Enable a Bedrock Guardrail on the endpoint so bad JSON is filtered as PII

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.3 names JSON for Bedrock and structured data for SageMaker endpoints. Same idea as InvokeModel: structured data in, bytes the endpoint expects. Converse does not wrap a SageMaker /invocations body.

incorrectExplanations.b: Converse is Bedrock Runtime. It does not become the serializer for a SageMaker container.
incorrectExplanations.c: AppConfig can hold the endpoint name. It does not map fields into the container contract.
incorrectExplanations.d: Guardrails sit on Bedrock model I/O. They do not parse SageMaker content types.

questions.scenario: Glue Data Quality scored a 10-K extract at 100%: ticker, period, and revenue exist and types match. The Lambda then sends the entire exhibit plus three years of history in one Converse user turn. The chosen FM’s context window is smaller than that payload. Bedrock returns a validation error. Product says validation already passed so this is a model outage.
questions.question: What actually failed?

options.text: The lake ruleset, which must include maxTokens as a Glue column
Cross-Region inference, which is how Bedrock rejects oversized prompts
Model-request validation — modality, request shape, and token / context size — after the dataset was already valid
Provisioned Throughput, which is required before a context window applies

questions.explanation: Dataset-valid is not enough. Also ask: can this FM consume this input? Modality, content type, request shape, token / context size, file limits, conversation roles, required fields. Dataset valid → model-request valid → invoke. That is 1.3.1 meeting 1.3.3. A 400 that looks like a model failure is often a body you never sized.

incorrectExplanations.a: DQDL checks lake columns (completeness, type, uniqueness). Context windows are an FM constraint, not a Glue column.
incorrectExplanations.b: CRI is spare Regional capacity for the same FM (1.2). It is not a prompt-size validator.
incorrectExplanations.d: PT is a capacity SKU. It does not change whether the payload fits the window.

questions.scenario: Analyst notes in the corpus sometimes include phone numbers and personal emails. The desk wants those redacted and `ticker=NVDA` tagged on each paragraph before the text is ingested into a Knowledge Base. They are not asking to block “buy NVDA” on a live Converse call. The cheapest tool that has a determinate NLP answer should win.
questions.question: Where does that enhancement run?

options.text: A Bedrock Guardrail on Converse, because PII is always a Guardrail
Amazon Macie as the Knowledge Base chunker
A fine-tune so the FM refuses to echo phone numbers from the index
Amazon Comprehend on the way in — entities / PII as input enhancement, then ingest the cleaned text

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.4: NLP enrichment is Comprehend — entities, language, sentiment, PII. Tag ticker or redact a phone number before the text hits a Knowledge Base. That is input enhancement, not RAG, and not a Guardrail. Guardrails sit on model I/O.

incorrectExplanations.a: A Guardrail filters the model call. It does not clean the corpus before retrieval. Comprehend on the way in is not a Guardrail.
incorrectExplanations.b: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3. It is not the KB ingest enhancer.
incorrectExplanations.c: Do not fine-tune to redact PII that should never have been indexed. Enhancement is cheaper and determinate.

questions.scenario: Incoming notes write `Q1 FY27` and `$26.0 billion`. The pipeline must emit `fiscal_year=2027, quarter=1` and `amount=26.0, unit=USD_BILLION` before embed. A developer proposes Converse on every row “so the model can interpret messy finance language.” The mapping is already a closed dictionary.
questions.question: Which enhancement is the cheapest determinate answer?

options.text: AWS Lambda (or equivalent code) for deterministic normalization — do not pay an FM to look up a ticker calendar
Amazon Bedrock on every row, because any rewrite is semantic transformation
Amazon Transcribe, because fiscal quarters are speech
SageMaker Processing, because normalization is always a 500 GB job

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.4: three categories — Lambda for deterministic normalization, Comprehend for NLP, Bedrock when code cannot parse the note. Use the cheapest tool that has a determinate answer. `NVIDIA Corporation` → `NVDA` and `Q1 FY27` → year/quarter are code.

incorrectExplanations.b: Semantic transformation is for messy analyst notes that become sections or themes when code cannot parse them. A closed fiscal calendar is not that job. You would also keep RAW vs DERIVED if you did use an FM.
incorrectExplanations.c: Transcribe is speech-to-text. These fields are already text.
incorrectExplanations.d: Processing is the scale kitchen, not the enhancement category. A dictionary map does not become Processing because the word “normalize” appeared.

questions.scenario: A Bedrock job rewrites messy analyst notes into normalized sections (DERIVED / AI-ENRICHED). A teammate wants to overwrite the RAW S3 object with that rewrite so the Knowledge Base has “only clean text.” Last month the rewrite dropped a risk-factor paragraph and nobody could prove what the filing originally said.
questions.question: How should provenance be kept?

options.text: Overwrite RAW with the LLM copy and keep a Slack screenshot of the job id
Keep RAW → CURATED → DERIVED / AI-ENRICHED as separate objects so a bad transformation still leaves the filing
Fine-tune on the rewrite so the original 10-K can be deleted from S3
Store only the embedding; lineage is implied by the vector

questions.explanation: Skill 1.3.4: do not overwrite the raw source with an LLM-normalized copy. Keep provenance RAW → CURATED → DERIVED / AI-ENRICHED. When the transformation is wrong, you still have the filing. Lineage of generated content is a later governance skill; the pipeline rule is: do not destroy the source.

incorrectExplanations.a: A screenshot is not an object store. Overwrite is how last month’s dropped paragraph became unprovable.
incorrectExplanations.c: Weights are not a filing archive. Deleting S3 because you fine-tuned is the opposite of provenance.
incorrectExplanations.d: An embedding is a derived index (1.4), not a substitute for the 10-K. If the index disappears you rebuild; if the source disappears you have a problem.

questions.scenario: A new hire thinks Amazon Bedrock is a GPU box you size in the account, like a SageMaker endpoint. The NVDA desk just needs Converse: send a paragraph, get four bullets, pay when they call. Nobody is patching CUDA.
questions.question: What is Bedrock Runtime, and how does the default SKU bill?

options.text: A cluster of GPU instances you pick (ml.g5.12xlarge); you pay instance hours whether anyone queried
A managed API in front of foundation models; on-demand Converse bills input tokens plus output tokens against a per-model per-Region quota
A vector database; you pay OpenSearch Compute Units to keep k-NN warm
A fine-tuning service only; inference is always SageMaker

questions.explanation: Bedrock is an API, not a box in your account. You enable a model and call Bedrock Runtime (prefer Converse). Default capacity is on-demand: pay input + output tokens, shared quota per model per Region, Too many requests at the ceiling. SageMaker is the kitchen when you must size GPUs or host your own image.

incorrectExplanations.a: That is a SageMaker (or EKS/EC2) instance. Bedrock hides the GPUs. You do not pick ml.g5 for a Converse PoC.
incorrectExplanations.c: Vectors live in S3 Vectors, OpenSearch, pgvector, DynamoDB, or a Knowledge Base backend. Bedrock Runtime is the FM call.
incorrectExplanations.d: Fine-tuning is one Bedrock/SageMaker job type. The everyday product is inference — Converse / InvokeModel — billed as tokens unless you buy Provisioned Throughput.

questions.scenario: Analysts must cite this quarter’s 10-K, not the model’s memory. Filings already sit in S3. The team wants managed chunk → embed → retrieve, then generate, without standing up their own index on day one.
questions.question: Which Bedrock product is that librarian?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases — managed RAG over your data source; the vectors may be Bedrock-managed or a store you name
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails — they retrieve the 10-K because a denied topic needs a citation
Amazon Macie — classification jobs are how AWS implements RAG
Amazon Q Developer — IDE completions over the 10-K bucket

questions.explanation: A Knowledge Base is Bedrock’s managed RAG layer: ingest, index, retrieve (and often retrieve-and-generate). You pay for embeddings/ingest plus the FM tokens on generate. The shelf underneath can be managed or OpenSearch / Aurora / S3 Vectors / Neptune / a third-party store. It is the librarian, not always the only store.

incorrectExplanations.b: Guardrails are a named policy on model input and output (topics, PII, jailbreaks). They do not index S3 filings.
incorrectExplanations.c: Macie finds sensitive data in S3. It is not a retriever.
incorrectExplanations.d: Q Developer is prebuilt IDE/PR assistance (2.5). Q Business is employee chat over company docs. Neither is the KB you wire to Converse for citations.

questions.scenario: Compliance wants “no investment advice” and no SSN echoed on the blotter. The check must run on the way into Converse and on the way out. They are not asking to redact the S3 corpus before ingest, and they are not asking for a homemade moderator Lambda wrapping the SDK first.
questions.question: Which product is the named policy on the model call?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend PII on the Knowledge Base, which is the same control as a Guardrail
AWS WAF on API Gateway, which reads prompt text for denied topics
SageMaker Clarify, which blocks investment advice at inference
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails — attach guardrailIdentifier + version on Converse; billed per policy evaluation on input and output

questions.explanation: A Guardrail is a named, versioned policy evaluated on the way in and the way out of the FM. You attach it on Converse (or Agents / KB generate). Pricing is per text unit processed by the guardrail, independent of the FM token bill. Comprehend on the way *in* to a corpus is input enhancement, not this live filter.

incorrectExplanations.a: Comprehend can redact PII before ingest (1.3.4). That is not the Converse-time policy. Guardrails sit on model I/O.
incorrectExplanations.b: WAF is HTTP/web ACL. It does not understand denied investment-advice topics inside a Bedrock body.
incorrectExplanations.c: Clarify is bias / explainability (SHAP), not a content filter on Converse.

questions.scenario: On-demand Claude in us-east-1 returns Too many requests at the open. The desk still wants the same FM, still wants token pricing, and does not want to rent Model Units overnight. Legal allows another US Region to serve the call.
questions.question: What is Cross-Region inference, and how does it bill?

options.text: A second provisioned endpoint you pay by the hour in us-west-2
Intelligent prompt routing, which is extra quota for one model
An inference profile (us.… / eu.… / global) — Bedrock may serve the same FM from another Region in that geography; still input + output tokens
A custom model deployment ARN, which is how CRI is spelled for fine-tunes

questions.explanation: CRI is spare Regional capacity for the same foundation model. You pass an inference profile ID (us.anthropic.…). Billing stays on-demand tokens. Custom / fine-tuned models cannot use CRI. A Lambda that retries us-west-2 yourself is the same idea with you owning the retries.

incorrectExplanations.a: Provisioned Throughput is dedicated Model Units by the hour. That is the opposite of “still token-priced, do not rent overnight.”
incorrectExplanations.b: Prompt routing picks a small or large model in a family for cost/quality. It is not extra quota for one FM, and it is not Regional spare capacity.
incorrectExplanations.d: Custom Model Deployment is on-demand invoke of a supported custom model. Custom models still cannot use CRI.

questions.scenario: The blotter’s load is flat all day, including 3am batch recaps. Finance will pay for dedicated Bedrock capacity so the shared on-demand quota cannot 429 the overnight job. They are not trying to make a custom model on-demand, and they are not spreading one FM across Regions.
questions.question: What are you buying?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput — Model Units reserved by the hour; you pay whether the desk is busy
Cross-Region inference, because dedicated capacity is spelled us.…
Prompt caching, which reserves GPUs for the IR methodology prefix
OpenSearch OCUs, which are Bedrock’s unit of FM capacity

questions.explanation: Provisioned Throughput is dedicated Bedrock capacity: you commit to Model Units and pay by the hour (and you pay at 3am). Use it when load is stable enough to fill the reservation, or when a custom model has no on-demand path. Do not rent 24/7 MUs for a three-hour earnings spike.

incorrectExplanations.b: CRI is still token-priced spare capacity in another Region. It is not a reserved MU.
incorrectExplanations.c: Prompt caching discounts a repeated input prefix. It does not reserve GPUs.
incorrectExplanations.d: OCUs are OpenSearch Serverless search capacity, not Bedrock FM seats.

questions.scenario: A supported custom model (fine-tune) is ready in a Region that offers Custom Model Deployment. Traffic is spiky like the on-demand blotter. A teammate says custom models are “PT or nothing” and wants to buy Model Units for the weekend spike.
questions.question: What does Custom Model Deployment actually offer?

options.text: Cross-Region inference for fine-tunes, using a us.… prefix on the custom ARN
A SageMaker real-time endpoint that Bedrock rebrands; you still pick an instance type
Nothing — custom models can only run on Provisioned Throughput
Invoke the deployment ARN as modelId and pay on-demand tokens — PT remains the lever for dedicated capacity or unsupported custom paths

questions.explanation: Custom models are no longer PT-or-nothing. Where Custom Model Deployment is supported, you invoke the deployment ARN as modelId and pay tokens like on-demand. PT is still how you buy dedicated, predictable capacity, and the path when on-demand custom is not offered. Custom models still cannot use CRI.

incorrectExplanations.a: CRI is for base FMs via inference profiles. Fine-tunes do not get us.… spreading.
incorrectExplanations.b: CMD is a Bedrock on-demand path for a custom artifact, not “pick ml.g5.” SageMaker endpoints are a different kitchen.
incorrectExplanations.c: That used to be the exam slogan. The current product split is CMD (variable traffic, supported) vs PT (dedicated / otherwise).

questions.scenario: Most blotter prompts are easy (“four bullets”). A few are hard compares. The team wants Bedrock to pick Haiku vs Sonnet in the same family at ask time to cut the token bill, without buying extra quota and without training a student model.
questions.question: Which offering is that runtime pick?

options.text: Cross-Region inference — Region is how Bedrock spells easy vs hard
Intelligent prompt routing — two supported models plus a fallback; easy → small, hard → large; still token-priced
Distillation — Bedrock picks the student at ask time without a training job
Prompt caching — cached completions are how cheap vs expensive is chosen

questions.explanation: Intelligent prompt routing changes the *model* (same family) at runtime for cost/quality. CRI changes the *Region* for the same FM. Distillation trains a cheaper model beforehand. AppConfig routing is your own business logic. Routing is not extra quota.

incorrectExplanations.a: CRI is spare capacity for one FM. The writer does not change.
incorrectExplanations.c: Distillation is a training job: teacher generates, student imitates. It is the cost cousin of routing, not a runtime router.
incorrectExplanations.d: Caching stores the computed state of a repeated *prefix*. It does not cache the completion and does not pick Haiku vs Sonnet.

questions.scenario: Friday they want Haiku instead of Sonnet without shipping a new Lambda zip. The app contract stays generate(messages). Someone proposes hardcoding MODEL in 17 functions and “just redeploy.”
questions.question: Which AWS product holds the pointer?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows, because a graph is how you change modelId
SageMaker Model Registry, which is the only place a Bedrock modelId may live
AWS AppConfig (or Parameter Store) — prod / cheap / fallback aliases; flip config, then re-eval
Amazon S3 Select on a JSON file in the Lambda package

questions.explanation: AppConfig (or Parameter Store) is the dynamic model-selection product: the application stays generate(messages); the modelId lives in config. Friday’s swap is not a zip. You still re-run the eval set — Converse is a shared envelope, not identical models. Registry is for custom-model packages you can roll back.

incorrectExplanations.a: Prompt Flows are a drawn graph of prompts, KB, Lambda, conditions. Useful, not the modelId pointer for a Converse app.
incorrectExplanations.b: Model Registry versions custom artifacts and approval states. It is not where every Bedrock on-demand ID must live.
incorrectExplanations.d: A file in the zip is still a redeploy. That is the anti-pattern AppConfig exists to kill.

questions.scenario: The research archive is 80 million transcript embeddings. A PM pastes a Jensen line twice a week. Nobody will manage a cluster. They want to pay for storage and the queries they actually run, not a search desk that stays staffed at 3am.
questions.question: Which store matches that bill?

options.text: Amazon S3 Vectors — vector buckets and indexes; serverless k-NN; sub-second when cold, ~100 ms when warmer; IAM s3vectors
OpenSearch Serverless — OCUs are free when query QPS is near zero
RDS PostgreSQL + pgvector — instance hours stop when the PM logs out
DynamoDB + Lambda cosine over every item — the cheapest k-NN at 80 million rows

questions.explanation: S3 Vectors optimizes vector economics: huge pile, infrequent lookup, no cluster, pay for use. Warm ~100 ms, cold sub-second — not a sub-10 ms hot engine. OpenSearch bills OCUs to keep the desk ready. RDS bills instance hours. Lambda cosine is not an index.

incorrectExplanations.b: Serverless OpenSearch still pays OCUs for readiness. Right for high-QPS hybrid search, expensive for twice-a-week archive k-NN.
incorrectExplanations.c: RDS is an instance. Idle rent is the kill on an infrequent, no-infrastructure stem.
incorrectExplanations.d: Paging 80 million items to compute cosine is a ruler, not a store. Native DynamoDB vector indexes are for operational items already in the table, still the wrong shelf for this archive.

questions.scenario: Two hundred analysts hit the blotter during market hours. They need exact ticker `AVGO` *and* commentary that means “networking attach on AI clusters,” plus facets. Latency must stay low. S3 Vectors looked cheap in the archive PoC.
questions.question: What are you staffing, and how does it bill?

options.text: S3 Vectors alone — hybrid keyword + vector is a metadata filter
Amazon Kendra — it is the exam’s high-QPS hybrid engine
Amazon CloudSearch, billed per document
Amazon OpenSearch (Serverless or managed) — keyword + k-NN hybrid, aggregations; Serverless bills OCUs to keep the desk ready

questions.explanation: OpenSearch is the search engine: BM25, filters, aggregations, and vector k-NN, often fused (hybrid). Serverless means you do not patch nodes; you still pay OCUs. That bill is for a live desk, not an archive doorbell. You can later export an S3 Vectors snapshot into OpenSearch — point-in-time, not a live sync.

incorrectExplanations.a: S3 Vectors is infrequent k-NN plus metadata predicates. It is not the SKU-and-meaning high-QPS desk.
incorrectExplanations.b: Kendra is enterprise search with connectors/ACLs. The Domain 1 hybrid/LTR story on this exam is OpenSearch (and Bedrock rerank in 1.5).
incorrectExplanations.c: CloudSearch is the older managed search product, not the vector/hybrid answer here.

questions.scenario: Fundamentals already live in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL: ticker, revenue, quarter. Analysts want “chunks near this Jensen quote AND ticker = NVDA AND revenue > $20B” in one SQL statement. They will accept a database instance.
questions.question: Which offering adds nearness to that table?

options.text: S3 Vectors with a JOIN clause, because vector buckets speak SQL
The pgvector extension on Aurora / RDS PostgreSQL — a vector column plus distance ORDER BY next to the spreadsheet facts
Neptune Analytics, because any JOIN is GraphRAG
DynamoDB Streams, which turn SQL into k-NN

questions.explanation: pgvector adds a vector type and distance operators to PostgreSQL. That is the product when the stem wants SQL joins to facts you already keep in Aurora/RDS. You pay instance hours (and storage). S3 Vectors is not a SQL database. Neptune is GraphRAG (traverse relationships), not “AND revenue > 20B.”

incorrectExplanations.a: S3 Vectors filters metadata; it does not JOIN to an Aurora revenue column.
incorrectExplanations.c: Neptune Analytics combines vectors with graph traversal (NVDA → TSMC → CoWoS). A SQL fundamentals join is pgvector.
incorrectExplanations.d: Streams replicate item changes. They are not a similarity index.

questions.scenario: Nightly Glue ETL already catalogs millions of filing rows. The team wants declarative rules (column exists, complete, unique) that the job evaluates, a data quality score, and CloudWatch metrics when the score drops — not a new Lambda per check.
questions.question: What is AWS Glue Data Quality?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend’s tabular mode
SageMaker Data Wrangler renamed for production ETL
A Glue feature: DQDL rulesets on the Data Catalog / ETL, failing records, passed/failed metrics to CloudWatch
Bedrock Guardrails for CSV files

questions.explanation: Glue Data Quality is the lake validator. You write DQDL (ColumnExists, IsComplete, IsUnique, …), Glue returns a score, and you can alarm in CloudWatch / SNS and stop Step Functions ingest. You pay as part of Glue jobs (DPU/job time), not per FM token. Wrangler is interactive prep; Lambda is the tiny event map.

incorrectExplanations.a: Comprehend is NLP (entities, PII, sentiment) billed on text units. It does not score a Glue table’s uniqueness.
incorrectExplanations.b: Wrangler is the visual / little-code kitchen. Flows can later feed production; it is not DQDL on nightly ETL.
incorrectExplanations.d: Guardrails evaluate model I/O. They do not run ColumnExists on a Data Catalog table.

questions.scenario: IR drops a 90-minute NVDA MP3. The job is an exact searchable transcript so a *text* embedder can retrieve passages. They are not searching the waveform with Nova Multimodal Embeddings, and they are not asking BDA for a structured JSON blob.
questions.question: What does Amazon Transcribe do, and how does it typically bill?

options.text: Speech-to-text (batch or streaming); you pay for audio processed (seconds), then you own the text pipeline
Text-to-speech; it reads the 10-K aloud so Titan can hear it
OCR of scanned 8-Ks; billed per page
A vector store for MP3 bytes; billed like S3 Vectors

questions.explanation: Transcribe turns speech into text (batch jobs from S3, or streaming). Pricing is based on audio duration processed, with add-ons like PII redaction or speaker diarization. After that, a text FM / text embedder / KB is a separate bill. Same MP3 can instead go multimodal-native or through BDA — different products, different meters.

incorrectExplanations.b: Amazon Polly is text-to-speech. Transcribe is the opposite direction.
incorrectExplanations.c: That is Textract (per page). Audio is not a scanned form.
incorrectExplanations.d: Transcribe emits text (JSON/transcript). It does not index MP3 embeddings.

questions.scenario: Two jobs landed the same week: (1) OCR a single checked-box 8-K form and its tables; (2) turn 50,000 10-K PDFs into company / revenue / tables / summary JSON with GenAI. A teammate wants one logo for both.
questions.question: How do Textract and Bedrock Data Automation split, including the usual meter?

options.text: They are aliases; both bill per FM token on Converse
Textract is only receipts (AnalyzeExpense); BDA is only IDs
Use Titan Text Embeddings on PDF bytes for both jobs; fields fall out of the vector
Textract = OCR / forms / tables, typically per page; BDA = blueprint-driven multimodal extraction at document scale, billed for pages/documents you process

questions.explanation: Textract is OCR and structure (DetectDocumentText vs AnalyzeDocument for forms/tables; AnalyzeExpense / AnalyzeID are specialized). You generally pay per page. BDA is GenAI extraction/normalization to JSON/Markdown/HTML/CSV at pile scale — a different altitude and a document/page processing bill, not “embed the PDF.”

incorrectExplanations.a: Neither product is “just Converse.” You can send an image to a multimodal FM, but that is a third path (look at the exhibit), not OCR-at-scale or BDA blueprints.
incorrectExplanations.b: AnalyzeExpense / AnalyzeID are Textract APIs. BDA is not “IDs only.”
incorrectExplanations.c: Embeddings do not parse a 10-K into fields. That trap shows up on 1.3; it is still wrong as a billing/product story.

questions.scenario: The corpus needs ticker tags and phone-number redaction *before* Knowledge Base ingest. The team also considered running Sonnet on every paragraph “for NLP.” Budget wants the purpose-built meter.
questions.question: What is Amazon Comprehend in this pipeline?

options.text: A Bedrock Guardrail with a different name; billed per Converse call
Managed NLP (entities, PII, language, sentiment) billed on text processed — cheaper determinate enhancement than an FM rewrite
The Glue Data Quality engine for unstructured text
Amazon Lex, which extracts entities only inside a chatbot

questions.explanation: Comprehend is input enhancement: entities, PII, language, sentiment. You pay for the text units you send, not for Sonnet tokens. It is not a Guardrail (those sit on model I/O) and not RAG. Use an FM only when code/Comprehend cannot parse the note — and keep RAW vs DERIVED.

incorrectExplanations.a: Guardrails filter the live model call. Comprehend cleans or tags the corpus on the way in. Different product, different bill, different moment in the pipeline.
incorrectExplanations.c: Glue Data Quality is DQDL on cataloged / ETL data. Unstructured NLP is Comprehend.
incorrectExplanations.d: Lex is conversational bots. Entity slots in a voice/chat skill are not corpus tagging.

questions.scenario: If Converse 429s three times, call the AppConfig fallback model; if that dies, return last night’s cached summary. The path is already written down. A developer wants an agent “so the model can decide to retry.”
questions.question: Which product runs that deterministic failover, and what are you paying for?

options.text: Bedrock Agents — ReAct is how AWS spells if/then retries
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler only — a cron is a circuit breaker
AWS Step Functions — you specify retries, backoff, fallback, degrade; billed per state transition, not per agent thought
Amazon SageMaker Pipelines, which is the inference circuit breaker

questions.explanation: Step Functions is the scripted workflow: retry with backoff, then fallback, then degrade. You pay per state transition (and standard vs express). Agents are for when the *model* must choose tools. Prompt Flows are a drawn Bedrock graph (prompts, KB, Lambda, conditions) — related idea, different product. A circuit breaker sits in front of CRI; it does not replace CRI.

incorrectExplanations.a: An agent decides tools in a loop. “If the API fails three times, call backup” is not a tool-choice problem. You would also pay FM tokens for the agent’s thoughts.
incorrectExplanations.b: Scheduler is a clock (every N minutes). Failover on a 429 is event-driven in the request path, not a cron.
incorrectExplanations.d: SageMaker Pipelines orchestrate ML training/deploy jobs. Not the live Converse failover path.

questions.scenario: An AMD research copilot always retrieves two 10-K exhibits, summarizes them, and emits JSON. The model never chooses a tool. A teammate labels it “agentic” because it calls Bedrock.
questions.question: The model never chooses a tool. The path is always retrieve, summarize, then JSON. What is this system?

options.text: A workflow with an LLM inside — the next action is predetermined
An agent — any Bedrock call is agentic
MCP — JSON output is a tool protocol
Multi-agent specialization — retrieve and summarize are two agents

questions.explanation: Agentic means the model chooses the next action from a goal and current state. A fixed retrieve → summarize → JSON path is a workflow, even if an FM generates the prose.

incorrectExplanations.b: Invoking a model is not the same as a decide/act/observe loop.
incorrectExplanations.c: JSON is a payload shape, not MCP.
incorrectExplanations.d: Two steps in one pipeline are not two agents.

questions.scenario: During an AMD run the process has ticker=AMD, valuation_complete=false, tools_called=7. The current model call includes the last tool result. Last month the analyst said they prefer an explicit bear case.
questions.question: Which mapping of run progress, last tool result, and analyst preference is correct?

options.text: Run progress is context; preferences are IAM
Store the analyst’s hunch “AMD will outperform” as a FACT in long-term memory
Run progress is state; the last tool result is context; the bear-case preference is long-term memory
All three are long-term memory

questions.explanation: State is where this execution is. Context is what the model can see this inference. Memory is what you intend to keep — typed as preference, not as a research fact.

incorrectExplanations.a: IAM is permission, not a memory layer.
incorrectExplanations.b: Opinion must not be retrieved later as evidence.
incorrectExplanations.d: Collapsing state, context, and memory is the 2.1.1 failure mode.

questions.scenario: A new AWS account in 2026 needs a managed agent loop (model + tools + instructions) for AMD research. A teammate starts CreateAgent on Bedrock Agents Classic.
questions.question: A new 2026 account needs a managed agent loop. A teammate starts CreateAgent on Bedrock Agents Classic. What should you do?

options.text: Classic is in maintenance mode and closed to new customers; use AgentCore Harness (or code on Runtime) and Gateway for tools
Use Textract as the orchestrator
Fine-tune instead of tools
Correct — Classic is the current default for greenfield agents

questions.explanation: Bedrock Agents Classic is maintenance-mode as of 30 July 2026. Exam stems may still say action groups. New architectures use AgentCore.

incorrectExplanations.b: OCR is not an agent loop.
incorrectExplanations.c: Customization does not replace tool use.
incorrectExplanations.d: Outdated for greenfield accounts.

questions.scenario: You wrote a Strands agent in Python. You need session isolation, identity, and managed hosting — not a second definition of the ReAct loop.
questions.question: You already have a Strands agent in Python. Which AgentCore piece hosts that code?

options.text: AgentCore Runtime
AgentCore Gateway
AgentCore Policy
Bedrock Agents Classic action groups

questions.explanation: Runtime hosts the agent you wrote. Gateway is the tool front door. Policy authorizes tool calls. Classic is the old managed loop.

incorrectExplanations.b: Gateway exposes APIs/Lambdas as MCP tools; it does not host your Strands process.
incorrectExplanations.c: Policy evaluates tool calls at the gateway.
incorrectExplanations.d: Classic owns the loop; you are bringing your own.

questions.scenario: Forty specialist agents. Incoming AMD questions must be classified, routed, and keep conversation context across handoffs. Leadership asks which AWS *managed service* that is.
questions.question: Which statement about AWS Agent Squad is most accurate on this exam?

options.text: Exam wording is AWS Agent Squad — it is an open-source router/supervisor, not a managed service; you host it (often on AgentCore Runtime)
Agent Squad is a managed AWS service with an SLA like AgentCore
Knowledge Base chunking routes specialists
Textract classifies earnings vs valuation

questions.explanation: Classification + routing + context is the supervisor / Agent Squad pattern. Squad is open source (exam still names it). AgentCore is the managed operations platform you might run it on.

incorrectExplanations.b: Do not treat an OSS framework as a metered AWS service.
incorrectExplanations.c: Chunking is retrieval, not specialist routing.
incorrectExplanations.d: OCR is unrelated.

questions.scenario: Product wants autonomous AMD research because the next source depends on evidence. The proposed design is only a Step Functions graph with InvokeModel states and no agent loop.
questions.question: A teammate says Step Functions is just another agent. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Nothing — Step Functions is always the agent
They should use Textract instead
They should fine-tune instead of retrieving
Incomplete — Step Functions bounds and sequences named transitions; it does not dynamically choose unnamed research actions

questions.explanation: Durable workflow ≠ agent. Often the agent runs *inside* the machine. Step Functions is the 2.1.2 answer when transitions should be explicit (approve → publish), not when the research path is unknown.

incorrectExplanations.a: Classic trap. The state machine is not intelligence.
incorrectExplanations.b: Unrelated.
incorrectExplanations.c: Unrelated.

questions.scenario: An AMD agent looped for 40 minutes with no recorded tool names. Debug is impossible. Leadership wants “chain-of-thought stored for audit.”
questions.question: The agent dumps the full chain-of-thought into DynamoDB as memory. What should you persist instead?

options.text: Only the final paragraph
